$comment: Logic subsystem: the off-the-shelf small-scale and medium-scale silicon on the C64 ASSY 250407 mainboard. Scope is the merchant 74-series TTL glue plus the few CMOS logic parts the board also used. Custom NMOS (6510, VIC-II, SID, CIA, PPI, PLA, ROMs) and discrete semiconductors are NOT covered here. Shared ids referenced from other files: metal.silica, metal.aluminum, metal.copper, metal.gold, metal.silver, metal.nickel, metal.chromium, chem.photoresist, chem.silane, chem.trichlorosilane, facility.water, facility.nitrogen, facility.argon, facility.electricity.

roots.name: 74-series glue logic
roots.description: The eleven off-the-shelf logic chips on a Commodore 64 ASSY 250407 that are not Commodore's own designs. They do no arithmetic and no video: they multiplex addresses, latch bytes, decode chip selects, count, generate the video dot clock and invert the cassette port. Nine are 74-series bipolar TTL in black epoxy DIP; three are CMOS; one is an older non-Schottky 7406. Individually each was a commodity costing tens of cents.
roots.note: The part list below is taken from the official C64 Service Manual parts list for PCB assembly #250407 and independently corroborated by three hobbyist references (Retrogate's retro.rewind wiki, the C64-Wiki motherboard page, and MonkeySpeak's hardware detail sheet). It is NOT the list the project brief suggested (74LS157, 74LS165, 74LS161, 74LS138, 74LS32, 74LS02, 74LS20, 74LS10, 74LS11, 74LS125, 74LS181, 74LS14, 74LS04, 74LS00) - that list belongs to the Apple II, the VIC-20 and the BBC Micro, not the C64. One widely-copied web page (oldsilicon.com) swaps the 74LS257 and the 74LS373 between U14 and U26; the service manual says U14 = 74LS258 and U26 = 74LS373, which this tree follows.

children.name: 7406 hex inverter buffer, open collector (U8)
children.description: Six inverting buffers whose outputs are open collectors rather than totem poles, in a 14-pin DIP. On the 250407 they invert and buffer the 6510's cassette-port output lines (CASS MOTOR, CASS SENSE, CASS WRITE, CASS DATA) and the shared user-port / serial lines. Open-collector outputs with pull-ups are how those lines could be wired-OR and level-shifted without contention, and a pin that shorts to ground leaves the CPU reading the defined 'off' state rather than floating.
children.note: The service manual lists U8 as '7406 sub 7416'. Commodore also second-sourced it internally as the MOS house-number part 7707, and those MOS-made 'equivalent' parts are notoriously unreliable - a 7406/7707 failing high is a classic cause of a dead datasette or a stuck serial bus. Confidence is medium on the exact nets driven; high on the part number and function class.

children.name: 74LS257 quad 2-to-1 multiplexer (U13 and U25)
children.description: Two identical 16-pin packages, each holding four independent 2-to-1 data selectors with non-inverting outputs. They exist for one reason: the 4164 DRAMs are multiplexed parts with only nine address pins, taking a row address first and a column address a few hundred nanoseconds later on the same wires. The CPU has sixteen address bits to deliver, so eight of them have to be time-division multiplexed onto four wires. One 74LS257 multiplexes four bits; two are needed for eight.
children.note: A 74LS257 differs from a 74LS258 only in having totem-pole (push-pull) outputs instead of three-state outputs. This distinction is why U13/U25 and U14 do different jobs.

facts.label: Select inputs per mux
facts.value: 4 (A, B, and shared select per nibble)

children.name: 74LS258 quad multiplexer with three-state outputs (U14)
children.description: The same four 2-to-1 selectors as the 74LS257 but with outputs that can be switched into a high-impedance state. This is the bus arbiter for VIC-II memory access: when the VIC-II is allowed to take the bus, the multiplexer's outputs are disabled so the VIC-II's own address pins can drive directly instead of fighting them. A failed U14 shows up as the VIC-II being unable to fetch screen data from RAM.
children.note: Some third-party board listings incorrectly give U14 as a 74LS373. The Commodore service manual parts list for #250407 says 74LS258.

children.name: 74LS139 dual 1-of-4 decoder (U15)
children.description: Two independent four-way decoders with common active-low enables and active-low outputs, in a 16-pin DIP. Given four address bits and an enable, each half asserts exactly one of four outputs. Commodore uses it to expand the sparse decode coming out of the PLA into individual chip selects - VIC-II banking, the I/O devices - and to qualify them with the read/write phase. Commodore also second-sourced it internally as the house-number part 7708/7711.
children.note: Part number and quantity are high confidence (service manual). The exact set of selects it generates is medium confidence because most of the C64's address decoding lives in the 82S100 PLA at U17, and secondary sources disagree about which outputs the 74LS139 finishes off. MOS house-number versions of this decoder were a notorious C64 failure; they are more fragile than the TI/Fairchild/National parts.

children.name: 74LS373 octal D latch, three-state (U26)
children.description: Eight transparent D-type latches with three-state outputs in a 20-pin DIP. The VIC-II has only eight address pins but must reach two different memories - the 1 KB screen/bitmap RAM and the character-generator ROM - so it puts one byte on its own pins while this latch holds the other byte. The three-state outputs let the CPU read the latched byte back whenever the VIC is not driving. A dead U26 corrupts text and bitmap graphics but leaves everything else alive, which is why it is the classic 'screen is garbage but the machine boots' fault.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: octal transparent latch with three-state outputs

children.name: 74LS08 quad 2-input AND gate (U27)
children.description: Four independent two-input AND gates in a 14-pin DIP - the most ordinary chip on the board and the one that does the most unglamorous work. ANDing is how the machine makes qualified control signals: a decode line ANDed with a clock phase becomes /RAS, /CAS or /WE for the DRAMs, and ANDed with the read/write phase becomes the chip select for the VIC-II, SID or CIA. Commodore also second-sourced it as house-number part 7712.
children.note: Part number and quantity are high confidence. The specific AND terms are inferred from the topology of a dynamic-RAM controller rather than read off the schematic net by net, hence medium.

children.name: 74LS74 dual D-type flip-flop (U29)
children.description: Two positive-edge-triggered D flip-flops with asynchronous preset and clear, in a 14-pin DIP. In the C64 they sit in the DRAM timing chain: shaping and stretching the column strobe and dividing or retiming the phase clock so the 4164s get a valid /CAS pulse on the right edge. A flip-flop is what turns a combinational AND into a one-shot wide enough to meet the memory's timing spec.
children.note: Part number and quantity are high confidence. The functional description is low confidence: hobbyist references variously call U29 a 'divider', a 'dual D-type flip-flop', and part of the VIC-II raster timing, and I did not trace the 251138 schematic net by net to settle it.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: dual D positive-edge-triggered flip-flop with preset and clear

children.name: 74LS193 synchronous 4-bit up/down counter (U30)
children.description: A four-bit presettable binary counter with separate up and down clocks and a clear, in a 16-pin DIP. It sequences the multiplexed dynamic-RAM cycle - stepping through address states and generating the refresh strobes - and helps step the VIC-II's raster counters. This is the chip that turns 'one address bit is high right now' into 'we are on the nth step of a cycle'.
children.note: Part number and quantity are high confidence (service manual). Its exact role is low confidence: sources call it a 'binary counter', a divider, and part of the clock-generation chain, and the 250407 does share a cluster of counters and flip-flops (U29/U30) around the DRAM and raster timing that is hard to allocate from the parts list alone.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: synchronous presettable 4-bit up/down binary counter with clear

children.name: 74LS629 dual voltage-controlled oscillator (U31)
children.description: Two voltage-controlled oscillator sections plus an enable and a range control, in a 14-pin DIP. The C64 has no crystal governing its video dot clock: one half of U31 amplifies the colour-subcarrier reference coming out of the video circuitry, the other half generates a free-running dot clock whose frequency is pulled by a control voltage. That is the oscillator half of the phase-locked loop completed by the MC4044 at U32. Despite the 'LS' prefix this part is CMOS internally, not bipolar TTL.
children.note: Part number, position and PLL role are high confidence and corroborated by scope measurements of the 250407 clock circuit published at tech.guitarsite.de/c64_scope.html. That the 74LS624-629 family is fabricated in CMOS rather than bipolar TTL despite the LS prefix is medium confidence: the family descends from Signetics/National designs and behaves like CMOS in pinout and power-up, but I did not find a period datasheet sentence stating the process. Some vendors did not offer it at all, which is itself suggestive.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: dual voltage-controlled oscillator with enable and range control

children.name: CMOS logic on the board: 4066 switches and MC4044
children.description: Four of the C64's glue chips are CMOS rather than bipolar TTL: two 4066 quad bilateral switches (U16, U28) and one MC4044 phase/frequency comparator (U32), plus the 74LS629 above. The 4066 is four independent CMOS transmission gates used as analogue multiplexers to route luma, chroma and audio and to hand the shared pins between the VIC-II and the outside world. The MC4044 compares the VCO's phase against the colour-subcarrier reference and generates the control voltage that locks the dot clock. Both were Motorola/RCA 4000-series parts, normally sold as CD4066B and CD4044B.
children.note: These are 4000-series CMOS, not 7400-series, so strictly they sit outside a '74-series' scope. They are included because they are the clearest demonstration that a single 1983 Commodore board carried two completely different semiconductor processes, and because the brief asked for the CMOS branch to be covered from a real machine.

facts.label: Named suppliers
facts.value: Motorola (MC prefix), RCA/Intersil (CD prefix), TI CD-prefix

children.name: LM556 dual timer (U20) - adjacent, not a logic part
children.description: Two 555-class monostable timers sharing one package, in a 14-pin DIP. It sits in the analogue paddle-input path, producing the timed pulse whose width the SID measures to report joystick and paddle position. Included here for completeness because it is off-the-shelf, because it is bipolar, and because it was made on the same diffusion lines as the TTL glue - just a different circuit on them.
children.note: An analogue bipolar part, not a 7400-series logic IC. Its internal process is a linear bipolar flow (epitaxial, deep base, wide-area emitters) rather than the Schottky-clamped logic flow described under mb.logic.bipolar.

children.name: Famous 74-series parts that are NOT on a C64
children.description: A warning about the part list. Frequently published lists of '74-series chips in the Commodore 64' include 74LS157, 74LS165, 74LS161, 74LS138, 74LS32, 74LS02, 74LS20, 74LS10, 74LS11, 74LS125 and 74LS181. None of those are on the ASSY 250407. They belong to other machines - the 74LS181 and 74LS181 look-ahead carry chips and the 74LS165 shift registers are Apple II parts, the 74LS157 multiplexers are VIC-20 and BBC Micro parts - and they are almost always the result of copying a generic 'TTL in home computers' list rather than reading a parts list.
children.note: Stated explicitly so the reader can trust the rest of this branch. The parts that really are fitted are the twelve listed in the sibling nodes. Which machine each wrong part belongs to is medium confidence.

children.name: The black epoxy DIP
children.description: Nearly every 74-series chip Commodore bought arrived in a black moulded dual in-line package: a lead frame carrying sixteen to twenty pins on 0.1 in centres, a piece of die glued to the frame's centre paddle, a fan of 0.5 mil gold wires, and about a third of a gram of filled epoxy poured over the whole thing and cured. This is the single most replicated package in electronics history.

facts.label: Row spacing
facts.value: 0.3 in (7.62 mm) for 14-24 pin; 0.6 in (15.24 mm) for 28/40 pin

facts.label: Bond wire
facts.value: 0.7-1.0 mil gold, ~20 bonds for a 20-pin DIP

children.name: Why 0.1 inch and 0.3 inch
children.description: The two dimensions that made the DIP work at all. The 0.100 in (2.54 mm) lead pitch was chosen so that a cheap single-row DIP socket, the same one used for the C64's own logic, could accept it. The 0.3 in (7.62 mm) row spacing was chosen so the body would just clear a 0.05 in hole-pad on 0.1 in centres and so a 14-pin part could be mounted on the older 0.6 in grid alongside the 40-pin parts. Wider bodies moved to 0.6 in rows.

children.name: 0.1 inch (2.54 mm) lead pitch
children.description: The distance between adjacent pins on one row of the DIP. It is the same pitch as the holes on a piece of perforated board, and it is the reason a 74LS04 could be dropped into a socket or a perfboard without any special tooling. The pin itself is a 0.25 x 0.5 mm rectangular wire, the narrow dimension facing the chip.

facts.label: Lead length (DIP-14)
facts.value: ~7.6 mm from body shoulder to tip

children.name: 0.3 inch row spacing and its wider variants
children.description: The distance between the two rows of pins. Standard JEDEC practice in 1983 was 300 mil for packages up to 24 pins and 600 mil for 28-pin and 40-pin parts, so a 40-pin device and a 16-pin device could share a footprint grid. A 900 mil (22.9 mm) body was used by some hermetic and high-current ceramic parts but was never common in merchant logic.
children.note: The 0.3 in / 0.6 in rule is high confidence; the existence of a 0.9 in (22.9 mm) row spacing in the same era is medium confidence - such spacings appear on hermetic and high-power ceramic packages, but I did not confirm one on a merchant logic part.

children.name: Nickel-iron lead frame
children.description: A continuous strip of metal, punched and formed into a repeating chain of DIP skeletons joined by tie-bars. It arrives at the assembler as a reel of maybe 3000 frames; the frames are cut out one at a time, plated, and then become the skeleton of the package - the seventeen or more separate pins, the two rows, and the little central ledge the die sits on.
children.note: Carpenter 45 (42% Ni / 58% Fe, balance carbon and manganese) and similar low-expansion nickel-iron alloys were the standard logic lead frame material because the thermal expansion coefficient was tuned to match the alumina-and-epoxy package, so the die, the frame and the mould compound do not fight each other over temperature cycling. It was a commodity ferronickel-like alloy made in ordinary steel melts.

children.name: The iron half of the lead frame alloy
children.description: Most of a logic lead frame by weight is iron, not nickel. The nickel - typically 42 percent, a little over a fifth of the mass - is the expensive part that tunes the expansion coefficient; the iron is commodity steel and was bought on the open market.

children.name: Iron ore for the frame alloy
children.description: The lead frame melt started life as steel, and the steel started life as ore. Two ores dominate: hematite (Fe2O3, the red ore) and magnetite (Fe3O4, the black ore). Both were shipped by rail and sea in bulk from the Lake Superior range, Mesabi and Labrador Trough, and the UK, and smelted in a blast furnace with coke and then converted.

children.name: Hematite (Fe2O3)
children.description: Iron in its fully oxidised state, typically 60-66 percent iron by mass, won by gravity concentration and magnetic washing of fine crushed ore. It was the dominant iron ore in world supply and the standard feed for a blast furnace.

children.name: Magnetite (Fe3O4)
children.description: The magnetic iron ore, ~72 percent iron and strongly ferrimagnetic, which is why it can be separated from gangue by a magnetic separator instead of by gravity alone. Much magnetite in 1983 came from taconite pellets shipped from the Mesabi range, a sintered concentrate rather than a lump ore.

children.name: Progressive-die stamping of the frame
children.description: The strip is fed through a sequence of steel dies on a mechanical press. Each station cuts, pierces, forms and bends a little more; by the last station the strip has a repeating row of completed DIP skeletons still joined by their tie bars. Ten to twenty tonnes of press capacity for a strip that is a tenth of a millimetre thick and has to be dimensioned to a few microns.
children.note: Photo-etched lead frames from copper and copper alloys were an alternative for high-lead-count parts, but the stamping route dominated through-hole logic DIPs in this period.

facts.label: Tie bars
facts.value: left until after the die is attached, to hold the frame rigid

children.name: The progressive die set
children.description: A stack of hardened tool-steel plates, each with apertures and forming punches cut by wire EDM or grinding, bolted into a set between the press bolster and the ram. Making the tooling for one frame number was a days-to-weeks job and was why a lead frame number was never changed casually: the tooling, the mould, the socket and the board artwork all had to change together.

children.name: Lead plating: tin, gold flash, nickel
children.description: Bare nickel-iron leads solder badly and gall when the DIP is pushed into and out of a socket, so every logic lead frame came out of the stamping press already plated. The common 1983 finish was an electroless or electrolytic nickel pre-plate followed by a matte tin or tin-lead overlay; gold flash over nickel was used where a part had to survive many insertions. A small fraction of frames used silver.
children.note: Matte tin plating on lead frames later became a reliability problem - tin whiskers - and the industry spent two decades fixing it. Copper-clad (C4) frames that carry a thicker, more solderable surface metal appeared in the late 1980s and 1990s, which is why the C64's successors used them and the C64 did not.

children.name: Tin plating bath
children.description: A chemical or electrolytic tin deposit, typically 1-3 micrometres thick, over a nickel underlayer. Tin is soft, wets solder readily and costs almost nothing, and it is why a logic chip could be soldered onto a two-layer board with a plain iron in an automated wave-solder machine with no special flux.

children.name: Cassiterite (SnO2) - the tin ore
children.description: Tin reached the plating tank as refined tin metal, made by carbothermic reduction of cassiterite, the tin oxide ore. In 1983 the world's tin supply came overwhelmingly from the Southeast Asian tin belt - Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand - and from Bolivia's Cerro Rico, and the price was famously volatile because the ore body was tiny in volume and the supply was political.
children.note: Malaysia, Indonesia and Bolivia were the dominant producers of tin in the early 1980s. The famous International Tin Council price collapse of 1985-86 - triggered by the release of stockpiles and by substitution - came just after the C64's peak production years.

children.name: Copper-clad C4 lead frame (later, not 1983)
children.description: A lead frame fabricated not from a bulk alloy strip but from an aluminium or copper leadframe clad on both faces with a controlled thickness of copper, so the surface the solder sees is copper rather than a flash plate. Known by the trademark C4. It solved the tin-whisker and solderability problems at once and became standard for fine-pitch packages from the late 1980s onward.
children.note: Included to mark the boundary: a C64 from 1983 contains no C4 frames. The technology existed in the late 1980s but was not standard on through-hole merchant logic.

children.name: The separated, tested die
children.description: Between the diffusion bay and the packaging line, the wafer is scribed into rectangles, diced, and every rectangle is probed while still in wafer form. The die that arrives at the assembly line is a bare rectangle of silicon, perhaps 1.5 by 2.5 mm, with a scratched pattern of aluminium bonding pads on one face and a bare oxide film over the circuitry on the other.

children.name: Scribing and dicing the wafer
children.description: A diamond stylus is dragged along the scribe lanes between dies, not to cut through but to fracture the crystal along the damage tracks buried in the oxide. For the narrow lanes the wafer is turned edge-on and run through a rotating diamond blade, or more recently a tensioned wire loaded with abrasive, which leaves far less chipping than a blade.

facts.label: Blade kerf
facts.value: ~0.15 mm for a resinoid dicing saw

children.name: The glass over the aluminium
children.description: After metallisation the whole wafer is coated in a thick film of silicon dioxide, usually with a plasma-deposited nitride cap. This passivation layer is what protects a 1983 logic die from the humidity and mobile ions that would otherwise creep under the aluminium and shift the threshold of a transistor. Openings in it are the bonding pads and the scribe lanes.
children.note: Early 1980s nitride deposition was increasingly low-pressure or plasma-enhanced CVD from silane and ammonia; furnaces using TEOS plus ammonia still ran in parallel.

children.name: Why 4164 DRAMs die but 74LS parts mostly do not
children.description: A 74LS gate is a handful of transistors with enormous margin; it either works or the diffusion is cracked. A 64Kx1 DRAM stores charge in a capacitor about 100 femtofarads across a transistor with a leakage path, and it has to be refreshed every few milliseconds. That is why the eight 4164s on the C64 are the board's failure-prone chips and the 74-series glue is almost always fine.
children.note: The mechanism (charge storage and refresh) is high confidence; the comparative failure rate is a well-attested field observation rather than a measured statistic.

children.name: Die attach, wire bond, moulding
children.description: Three operations turn a loose die and a loose lead frame into a component. The die is brazed to the frame's central ledge. Twenty-ish gold wires are ball- or wedge-bonded from pads on the die to the inner ends of the pins. Then about 0.3-0.5 g of filled black epoxy is transfer-moulded over everything and cured.

children.name: Die attach to the frame paddle
children.description: The die is placed face-down onto a small ledge in the middle of the lead frame and brazed there with a preform of gold-silicon eutectic at 350-400 C. The eutectic melts before the silicon itself does, so the joint is made without heating the chip to a temperature that would damage it. Cheap parts instead used a silver-filled organic paste cured on a hot plate, or conductive epoxy, and some logic used glass-frit die attach for thermal cycling.
children.note: Organic die attach became common in the late 1980s-90s for cost reasons. In 1983 Au-Si eutectic brazing was still the standard on logic and memory.

children.name: Gold wire bonding
children.description: A machine called a wedge bonder (or, for higher volume, a ball bonder) presses a hair-thin gold wire onto an aluminium bonding pad with a tungsten or ceramic tool while a hydrogen torch or arc welds them together, then repeats on the other end at the pin. Each joint is an intermetallic wedge of aluminium-gold, cut with a pulled wire rather than cut. It is the cheapest way ever devised to connect a chip to the outside world, and it is why every 1983 logic chip has that characteristic fan of gold legs.
children.note: Ball bonding, with a 2.5 mil wire and ~25-50 bonds per second, was displacing wedge bonding for high pin counts in this period. Wedge bonding at ~10 bonds per second dominated merchant logic.

children.name: The wedge bonder
children.description: A two-station machine that draws wire from a spool, forms a loop, drives a wedge onto the die pad under a hydrogen flame, swings 90 degrees, and drives the second wedge onto the pin, then snaps the wire. Twenty or forty of these sat in a row along a packaging line, each attended by one operator feeding frames in and taking packaged parts out.

children.name: Transfer moulding the black epoxy body
children.description: A slab of thermosetting epoxy loaded with 70-80 percent spherical silica is melted at 175 C and forced through a small orifice into a multi-cavity steel mould - the transfer mould - that holds the wired frame in one cavity per die. The compound flows around the wire loops, fills voids, and cures in three to five minutes. Because it is filled with silica it is not really a plastic in the loose sense: it is a ceramic-filled thermoset whose job is to hold the die in place, carry heat away, and keep moisture out.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 3-5 min in the mould, then a post-mould bake

children.name: The transfer press
children.description: A heated platen press with a pot and plunger that transfers melted compound into the mould. Modern machines are multi-cavity and run at thousands of shots an hour; a 1980s line used 20- to 100-shot multi-cavity tools and got through a few hundred thousand DIPs a month.

children.name: Epoxy moulding compound
children.description: A blend of roughly 15 percent resin system and 85 percent filler by weight. The resin is an epoxy-novolac cured by a phenolic novolac; the filler is spherical fused or precipitated silica graded from a few microns up to about 100 microns so the compound can be both thin enough to flow around a 25 um wire and stiff enough to survive handling; and there is a trace of carbon black pigment to make the part black, plus a trace of mould release. Green compounds arrived in the mid-1980s.

facts.label: Resin system
facts.value: epoxy cresol novolac + phenolic novolac hardener

children.name: Epoxy cresol novolac resin
children.description: The workhorse of chip packaging in every decade since 1970. Cresol-formaldehyde epoxy novolac is made from epichlorohydrin and a cresol-formaldehyde novolac; cured with a phenolic novolac and catalysed with a small amount of hexamethylenetetramine, it cures without volatiles and without ionising anything, so it does not damage the die. The epoxy end comes from epichlorohydrin, which came from propylene and chlorine, which came from salt and natural gas - so the plastic body of every 74LS chip traces back to crude oil.
children.note: Bisphenol A epoxy (the older, less package-friendly EPON-type system) was still used on some parts; cresol novolac had largely displaced it in logic packaging.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: phenolic novolac + hexamine, 175 C, no by-products

children.name: Epichlorohydrin (1-chloro-2,3-epoxypropane)
children.description: The bifunctional building block of every epoxy. Chlorohydrination of propylene (propene plus hypochlorous acid, with the propylene itself coming from the cracking of refinery hydrocarbons or of natural-gas liquids) gives 1,2-dichloropropane, and base dehydrochlorination closes the epoxide ring.

children.name: Propylene from the cracker
children.description: Steam cracking of naphtha or of natural-gas-propane. Propylene is the second most produced organic chemical in the world and the cheapest epoxide feedstock, which is why epichlorohydrin was always made from it and never from anything else.

children.name: Naphtha (light petroleum fraction)
children.description: The low-boiling cut of crude oil distillation, roughly C5 to C11. Everything in the chain from the epoxy moulding compound through to the solder mask and the photoresist binder starts in this fraction, because it is the cheapest feedstock with the right carbon skeleton.

children.name: Crude oil
children.description: The whole hydrocarbon trunk of the tree: the carbon in the package epoxy, the resist binder, the solder mask, the flex circuits and the petrol that moved it all.

children.name: Chlorine for the chlorohydrin step
children.description: Elemental chlorine from the chlor-alkali cell: brine electrolysed, producing chlorine, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen in one pass. The chlorine is reacted with water to make the hypochlorous acid, and the resulting dichloropropane is treated with caustic soda to open the epoxide.

children.name: Brine (concentrated sodium chloride)
children.description: Saturated salt solution, the feed for every chlor-alkali plant. It is the base of the entire chlorinated organic chemistry that runs underneath plastics, solvents, refrigerants and the photoresist industry - including the acid used to strip a wafer's photoresist after it has been used.

children.name: Rock salt (halite)
children.description: Sodium chloride, mined or dissolved from halite deposits and then evaporated from seawater in salt pans. Almost all industrial chlorine and almost all industrial sodium hydroxide in the world in 1983 came from this one rock.

children.name: Carbon black pigment
children.description: About half a percent by weight of furnace black, dispersed into the compound, to make the package opaque black. Black rather than natural-coloured because a black package hides internal voids, and because it was what the whole industry had standardised on since the first plastic DIP.
children.note: The pigment is a trivial mass fraction of the whole computer but it is the same furnace black that goes into the resistors and the toner's photoconductor.

children.name: Furnace black feedstock
children.description: Heavy petroleum residuum or natural gas fed to an air-cooled sooting furnace; the soot is scraped off water-cooled rotors and pelletised. It is chemically the same carbon black described in the resistor branch of this tree.

children.name: The mould cavity and ejector pins
children.description: A hardened, polished steel block with one to hundreds of identical cavities. For a DIP the cavity is a rectangle with fourteen to twenty pin-shaped slots; the mould also carries the moulded cavity number, the vendor's part-number embossing, and ejector pins that push the finished part out without scuffing it. Moulds lasted a few hundred thousand to a few million shots.

facts.label: Cavity marks
facts.value: the number 1 or a letter, moulded into the underside

children.name: Post-mould cure and stability bake
children.description: Moulding compounds are incompletely polymerised at the mould temperature. Parts are therefore baked for hours at 175 C afterwards, which completes the cure and drives off the last of the residual stress. It was a batch operation: thousands of parts in a tray, hours in a oven, on a schedule that ran overnight.

children.name: Probe test before packaging
children.description: Die that fail are thrown away before they are worth a lead frame. The wafer is loaded onto a probe stage, a probe card with one needle per bonding pad is lowered onto it, and a tester runs every pattern and every DC parameter. Only known-good die are cut. This is why probe test and not final test is what sets the economics of a logic wafer: a yield loss after packaging has already cost you the moulding and the wire bonds too.

children.name: The wafer probe station
children.description: A heavy cast stage that steps the wafer die by die under a fixed probe card: a vacuum or hot chuck on an x-y-z stage, a microscope to line the card up, and a needle interface to the tester. An operator loads a cassette of up to 25 wafers and unloads it at the end; everything in between was automatic.

children.name: The probe card
children.description: A ceramic or printed-circuit substrate carrying one cantilever needle per bonding pad, cantilevered down from an epoxy or quartz shell so the needles survive hundreds of thousands of touches on hard silicon. Building a card for a new part number took days and cost hundreds to thousands of dollars, which is why a device that sold for thirty cents could not afford a new probe card per variant.

children.name: The logic tester
children.description: An automated test system running a stored functional pattern and a set of DC limit tests per device type: propagation delay, fan-out current, input current, output high and low voltage, and the truth table at the functional corners. A 74LS04 has a few hundred such tests. The tester was the expensive part of probe test and was amortised across every device type on the line.

facts.label: Instrumentation
facts.value: TTL pattern generator, timing analyser, DC meter

children.name: The ceramic DIP (mostly not used here)
children.description: For military and extended-temperature parts the epoxy was replaced by a package made of alumina ceramic, sealed hermetically with a glass frit or a metal lid. It could be baked out, leak-tested, and taken from -55 to +125 C without the epoxy softening. It was also more expensive and much larger, so merchant logic in a home computer was always plastic: the C64's own 74-series parts are all black epoxy, with the ceramic version only appearing in industrial or aerospace equipment.
children.note: The 74LS series exists in both CDIP (ceramic) and PDIP (plastic) forms, distinguished by the letter after the temperature grade: N is plastic (0 to +70 C), E or M is ceramic (-55 to +125 C). Commodore specified N-grade parts.

children.name: Alumina ceramic body
children.description: A package shell made of 95-99 percent alumina, formed by pressing or by tape-casting a green body in a serpentine conductor pattern and firing it at 1500-1600 C. Alumina was chosen because it matches silicon and the glass seal closely in expansion, is cheap, and is a good thermal conductor compared with any polymer.

children.name: Bauxite, the alumina ore
children.description: Bauxite is the only commercial ore of aluminium, and alumina refined from it is both the ceramic used in ceramic packages and the feed for the aluminium metallisation on the die - two completely different routes to the same element, sitting a few centimetres apart on the same 74LS part.

facts.label: Main 1980s sources
facts.value: Jamaica, Suriname, Guinea, Australia, bauxite residue from Sines (Portugal)

children.name: Kovar lid and nickel seal ring
children.description: For parts sealed with metal rather than glass, a lid of Kovar (iron-nickel-cobalt, chosen for its matching expansion) is brazed or welded to a nickel ring around the ceramic. Kovar is the same idea as the lead frame alloy: pick the expansion coefficient of the metal so it matches the ceramic and the seal does not crack.

children.name: Glass frit sealing
children.description: A paste of powdered borosilicate glass with a small amount of binder is applied around the rim, the lid is set on it, and the assembly goes through a sealing furnace. The glass melts, wets the metallised ceramic and the metal lid, and on cooling forms a hermetic, dimensionally matched bond. The temperature profile - ramp, soak around 700-750 C, controlled cool - is the whole art of it.
children.note: Sealing in a continuous belt or pusher furnace at a few hundred degrees per hour rather than 700-750 C soak is the classic profile; the exact numbers vary by package. Medium confidence on the peak temperature.

children.name: Marking the top of the package
children.description: Ink printing was still the norm in 1983: a pad or a dot-matrix printer lays the part number, the manufacturer's mark, a date code (year and week, e.g. 8341) and a lot or assembly code on the moulded surface. Laser marking was beginning to appear, mostly for military parts, and would take over within a decade because a laser-marked part cannot be relabelled.
children.note: Commodore bought these chips from several vendors and did not re-mark them, which is why an original C64 board may carry parts branded TI, Fairchild, National, Motorola, Hitachi, Toshiba or a Commodore house number, all mixed together.

facts.label: Packaging of record
facts.value: tubed, then later dry-packed and taped

children.name: Marking ink
children.description: A phenolic or epoxy ink with a pigment, laid on and baked, or cured by UV or by laser ablation of the mould compound. Cheap and utterly routine - but it is why an original C64 chip is still readable today and a modern BGA is not.

children.name: Laser marking (emerging)
children.description: A Q-switched Nd:YAG or CO2 laser ablating characters into the epoxy surface, or a carbon laser removing the top layer to expose an underlying white layer. Fimeless, indelible and fast, but in 1983 it was still a premium option used mostly for military marking.
children.note: Adoption of laser marking on merchant plastic DIPs was well underway by the mid-to-late 1980s; in 1983 it was still a minority of parts.

children.name: How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)
children.description: The 74LS family was not built on the same kind of line as the Commodore custom chips. This is a junction-isolated, collector-diffused bipolar process: an n+ buried-and-collector structure grown epitaxially on p-type silicon, four thermal diffusion cycles, a sputtered NiCr resistor level, one level of aluminium metallisation, about eight mask levels and sixty to a hundred process steps. Minimum drawn features were 3-5 um - twenty times coarser than a 1983 dynamic RAM - which is exactly why a logic chip cost a fraction of what a 6510 or a 4164 cost.
children.note: This is a generalised description of the standard junction-isolated bipolar logic process as it was run in 1982-84 by TI, Fairchild, National and Motorola. Precise vendors differed: Fairchild also offered a dielectric-isolation variant, and TI ran some processes with ion implantation instead of thermal base diffusion. I have marked medium confidence rather than high because the 74LS flows are proprietary and I have not seen a period process description for a specific vendor's 74LS line. The transistor structure, the four-diffusion sequence, the NiCr resistor level and the eight mask levels are all well documented industry practice for the era.

facts.label: Diffusion cycles
facts.value: 4 thermal: isolation, base, emitter, plus the epitaxial growth itself

facts.label: Interconnect
facts.value: single aluminium level + sputtered NiCr resistor

children.name: The junction-isolated bipolar flow
children.description: The sequence that turns a plain slice of silicon into a chip of interconnected bipolar transistors. Four diffusion cycles do all the work: an n+ isolation diffusion to separate each transistor into its own island; a p base diffusion under the island to form the transistor base; an n+ emitter diffusion into the base to form the emitter; and the Schottky-barrier levels that give the 'LS' in 74LS its name. Between and inside those cycles sit an epitaxial growth, a thin-film resistor deposition, a metallisation and a passivation.

facts.label: Isolation
facts.value: n+ phosphorus, driven to the substrate

facts.label: Emitter
facts.value: n+ phosphorus or arsenic, Rs ~10-30 ohm/sq

children.name: p-type starting wafer
children.description: A slice of p-type silicon, lightly doped so that it is a good insulator between transistor islands and does not leak much reverse current. Everything the tree contains - the transistors, the resistors, the isolation - sits on this one piece of crystal.

children.name: Epitaxial growth of the collector
children.description: The single most distinctive step of the bipolar process. The wafer is placed in a horizontal reactor and a few micrometres of lightly doped n-type silicon is grown on top of it in a hydrogen atmosphere at about 1100-1200 C. The growing layer inherits the crystal lattice of the wafer below, so the n-type collector sits on the p-type substrate as a perfect single crystal - a vertical diode. Without epi, a vertical bipolar transistor would be impossible.
children.note: The reactor also dopes: phosphine or arsine is mixed into the hydrogen stream so the epilayer comes out n-type to a controlled resistivity. This is one of only two places (the other being the isolation and emitter diffusions) where a distinct dopant chemistry is needed.

children.name: The horizontal epitaxial reactor
children.description: A quartz or silicon-carbide tube with a graphite susceptor that is heated by a radio-frequency induction coil. Silane or trichlorosilane and hydrogen flow past; the silicon atoms deposit on the hot wafer. Inductors rotate the wafer and provide the radiant heat. Loaded by hand or by a cassette elevator; a batch of 20-30 wafers takes an hour or two.

children.name: Trichloroethylene-trichlorosilane vapour mix (not HCl)
children.description: The epitaxial gas box fed a mixture of silane or trichlorosilane in hydrogen, with dopant gas added for conductivity. Trichlorosilane is the workhorse chlorosilane of the period; silicon tetrachloride was the older, hotter source. The hydrogen carrier is dry and ultra-pure.

children.name: Phosphine (PH3) for the n-type epilayer
children.description: The dopant gas for the n-type collector and for the n+ isolation and emitter diffusions. A few parts per million of phosphine in the hydrogen carrier sets the resistivity. Phosphine itself is made by reacting phosphoric acid (from phosphate rock) or elemental phosphorus with hydrogen, or by burning phosphorus vapour.

children.name: Elemental phosphorus from phosphate rock
children.description: White phosphorus was produced by carbothermic reduction of calcium phosphate (apatite) with coke and silica in an electric furnace, then condensed to a waxy solid. Most phosphine was made by reacting this phosphorus with hydrogen or by hydrolysing phosphorus trichloride made from it.
children.note: White phosphorus production is the deep origin of the dopant gas in every n-type diffusion in this tree.

children.name: Phosphate rock (apatite)
children.description: Calcium phosphate ore, mainly from Florida, Morocco, Senegal and China. Reduced in an electric furnace with coke and silica to make white phosphorus, which is the only practical high-purity source of the phosphorus dopant.

children.name: Arsine (AsH3) - the shallow-diffusion dopant
children.description: A very shallow-diffusing dopant, used where a junction must stop just below a thin gate oxide without drifting deeper in the subsequent hot steps. Arsenic replaced antimony for this job as the physics improved. Arcsine came from arsenic trioxide (from roasting arsenic-bearing ores) plus hydrogen.
children.note: Arsenic was used on the bipolar emitters here and, on the CMOS side, for the n+ source/drain. Arsenic-bearing copper concentrates were a notorious long-time hazard in smelting, which is why arsenic control in copper works is a regulated topic today.

children.name: Arsenic trioxide from ore roasting
children.description: Arsenic occurs in some copper and lead ores as arsenide. Roasting the concentrate oxidises the arsenic to arsenic trioxide fume, which is captured and reduced to elemental arsenic, then combined with hydrogen to give arsine.
children.note: Arsenic is present in metal ores from the ancient earth; the specific separation path described is high confidence as industrial chemistry.

children.name: Growth of the field oxide
children.description: Silicon dioxide grown by passing steam over the wafer at 900-1050 C. This thick oxide is the field oxide: it covers everything except the windows that are later cut for diffusion and metallisation, and it is what electrically and physically isolates one transistor island from the next, in the same way the oxide isolates a MOS gate.

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: mask for diffusion + isolation + field-effect control

children.name: The oxidation furnace
children.description: A horizontal tube furnace, quartz or silicon-carbide, heated to 1000 C, with wet oxygen or steam flowing through. The wafer rides on a quartz boat pushed in and out by a loader. Oxidation is the slowest step in a bipolar line and the furnaces are the bottleneck.

children.name: Deionised steam for the furnace
children.description: Ultra-pure water turned to vapour in the furnace inlet. The water must be essentially free of dissolved alkali metals, because sodium diffuses fast through hot oxide and shifts a transistor's threshold. Fab water came from municipal supply through a chain of reverse osmosis and ion exchange.

children.name: Fused quartz tube and boat
children.description: The tube the wafer sits in is fused quartz, because quartz holds up to about 1100 C and is chemically inert to the oxidising atmosphere. Quartz is itself manufactured from high-purity silicon, so the tube and the silicon it processes came from related chemistry.

children.name: Collector-collector isolation
children.description: The first diffusion. Where the field oxide has windows, phosphorus is driven in to make a heavily n-doped region that runs all the way down to the p-type substrate. Everything inside a window is now n-type; the n+ walls around and between windows cut the wafer into separate n-type islands, each with a p substrate beneath it. Two n+ islands separated by a p-substrate region form back-to-back diodes, and those diodes are the isolation - a device made entirely of unwanted junctions doing an essential job.
children.note: The isolation junctions carry the full supply voltage between adjacent islands, so they are reverse-biased diodes and must be kept clean and leak-free. Guard rings and careful gettering protect them.

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: through the n-epilayer into the substrate

children.name: Diffusion into the window
children.description: The wafer is coated with a phosphorus-bearing dopant source - a spun-on emulsion or a deposited glass - then pushed into a furnace at 1000-1150 C. Heat alone moves the phosphorus atoms down into the silicon, opening up and closing the junction as it goes. Diffusion, not implantation, because diffusion gives the smooth graded junctions that give a transistor its gain.

children.name: Guard rings around the islands
children.description: A ring of n+ material, often tied to the most positive supply, laid around each sensitive island. It intercepts stray minority carriers and surface charge before they can reach the isolation junction, and it raises the breakdown voltage of the isolation. Guard rings are one of the oldest tricks in the planar process and were still drawn on a 1983 logic layout.

children.name: What a guard ring physically is
children.description: Not a new material - just the same n+ diffusion, but drawn as a closed loop around the transistor instead of a small dot. The mask for the isolation diffusion draws the guard ring at the same time as the island, so it costs one more shape on one mask and no extra process step. That is the whole elegance of it.

children.name: Dielectric isolation (the alternative, and Fairchild's route)
children.description: Instead of relying on reverse-biased isolation diodes, the islands can be sunk into a solid thermally grown oxide so each is completely surrounded by insulating oxide. The wafer is oxidised, then diffusion (or epitaxy) is done into small windows in the oxide; the oxide under the silicon is never removed, so no vertical isolation junction exists at all. This gives lower capacitance and better speed but is much harder to make, because the silicon has to be grown in a hole in oxide without lifting it.
children.note: Dielectric isolation was used by Fairchild and a few others for high-performance analog and for some logic families in the 1970s and 1980s, but junction isolation was cheaper and dominated standard 74LS. I could not confirm which isolation a given vendor's 74LS used; most 74LS parts are believed to be junction-isolated.

children.name: Deep trench isolation (later, and now extinct in logic)
children.description: For the highest-performance bipolar processes - the ones behind linear amplifiers and the last power logic - isolation was cut as a deep trench etched into the substrate and filled with oxide or polysilicon, then buried. This gives near-vertical isolation walls and far lower capacitance than the lateral isolation diffusion. It was expensive and it is now essentially extinct in merchant logic.
children.note: The brief asked for the deep-trench-isolation-came-later point. Confirmed: trench isolation appeared in high-performance bipolar through the 1980s and 1990s and is gone from the logic business entirely, because CMOS with shallow-trench isolation simply won.

children.name: The base diffusion
children.description: A second diffusion. Through a new mask, boron is driven into each n-island to make the p-type base of the transistor. The base is the thinnest and most tightly controlled region in the whole structure - roughly half to one micrometre deep - because the transistor's gain and its maximum speed both come from how narrow the base is. Every minute the base is too wide, the transistor is slow.

facts.label: Why thin
facts.value: base transit time sets transistor fT

children.name: Boron as the p dopant
children.description: Boron came from a thin deposited glass or oxide doped with boron (B2O3, often as diborane gas) spun onto the wafer and driven in. It was the standard p-dopant for base diffusions throughout the era.

children.name: Diborane (B2H6) gas
children.description: Boron hydride gas used as a diffusion or implantation source. It is pyrophoric and toxic, and shipped and handled in sealed steel cylinders under inert gas.
children.note: Boron trichloride (BCl3) was the other common boron gas source.

children.name: Borax / boron oxide source
children.description: For thermal diffusion, boron was often carried in a boron-doped oxide or a BN wafer placed face-to-face with the silicon in the diffusion boat. Cheaper and easier to handle than gas.
children.note: Solid-source BN and doped-oxide diffusion was the classic boron diffusion technique before diborane became routine.

children.name: The emitter diffusion - and the gold in it
children.description: The third diffusion. Through a finer mask, a very heavily doped n+ region is driven into the boron base, forming the emitter. Because the n+ emitter is so much more heavily doped than the p base, the emitter-base junction is forward-biased at only 0.7 V and injects enormous current gain - but only as long as the emitter does not punch through the thin base under the reverse bias of the collector. Pushing gold into the emitter diffuses the emitter junction forward slightly, making the junction harder for holes to reverse-inject, which suppresses punch-through and the associated capacitance, and raises the gain. This is the 'gold-doped emitter'.
children.note: The gold-doped (Au-doped) polysilicon emitter was a real and important technique of this era, used to raise gain and suppress the emitter-base reverse conductance ('knee'). It was implemented by co-depositing a tiny amount of gold in the emitter polysilicon or dopant glass, then driving it in with the arsenic or phosphorus. Confidence medium: the technique is well documented, but I have not confirmed that a specific 74LS vendor's 1983 process used it; it was common in high-performance bipolar rather than mandatory in low-cost logic.

facts.label: Gold purpose
facts.value: suppress emitter-base reverse leakage and push-through

children.name: The gold in the emitter
children.description: A fraction of a percent of gold, introduced by co-doping the emitter source and driven in with the emitter diffusion. Gold is a deep acceptor-diffusing substitutional impurity in silicon; it behaves in the base like a recombination centre. In the emitter-base junction it forward-shifts the junction for electrons and suppresses hole injection into the emitter, which is what raises gain and kills the reverse gain of the transistor.
children.note: Gold as a recombination centre in silicon is well established physics; its use in Au-doped emitters is a documented period technique. Exact concentration is on the order of a fraction of a percent in the emitter.

children.name: Polysilicon emitter (a later refinement)
children.description: Instead of diffusing the emitter through a mask, a thin polysilicon film is deposited, doped with arsenic, patterned to define the emitter, and then pushed. The arsenic is confined by the polysilicon walls so the emitter comes out shallower and more uniform, and the emitter area - which sets the emitter resistance - is set by the same mask as the metal that contacts it. This self-aligned polysilicon emitter was one of the last big improvements to the classical bipolar process before CMOS took the business.
children.note: Poly-emitter bipolar was widespread in analog ICs through the 1980s and 1990s. Whether a 1983 commodity 74LS used it is doubtful - it adds cost for a speed the LS family does not need.

children.name: The Schottky clamp - the S in LS
children.description: In standard 7400-series TTL a transistor saturates when it is driven hard: both junctions forward-biased, charge stored in the base, and the transistor slow to turn off. A 74LS puts a small Schottky diode - metal to lightly doped n-type, with no forward drop - from each transistor's base to its collector. When the base tries to go more forward than a silicon junction would allow, the Schottky diode conducts first and steals the excess, pinning the collector voltage just above saturation. The transistor never saturates, so it turns off in a couple of nanoseconds instead of twenty. That is the whole 'Schottky' idea, and it is why an LS gate is fast and still low-power.
children.note: The Schottky barrier itself is formed simply by touching aluminium to the lightly doped n-type collector (aluminium-silicon is 0.75 eV work-function difference against n-Si) - no extra mask beyond the one that defines the collector contact, because the Schottky diode and the ohmic collector contact are made in the same window. So the LS family costs the same number of mask levels as plain TTL. First commercial Schottky TTL was TI's 74S series, 1964.

facts.label: Barrier
facts.value: Al on n-type Si, ~0.75 eV work-function difference

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: prevents transistor saturation; 74LS gate delay ~10 ns

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: no extra mask - same window as the collector contact

children.name: The NiCr thin-film resistor level
children.description: A 74LS is full of resistors - the pull-ups, the current-limiting elements, the bias network. In a silicon-gate-era bipolar line they were made as a deposited thin film of nickel-chromium alloy, sputtered onto the wafer, patterned by one extra mask, and annealed. This is the one mask level that separates the 74LS flow from a plainer bipolar analog flow, and it is why an 'LS' logic wafer and an analog bipolar wafer had different mask counts.
children.note: Resistors in this class were 'thin film', not 'thick film': the NiCr was deposited in a vacuum (sputtered) to a controlled sheet resistance of order 100-250 ohm/square, then laser- or acid-trimmed to value. Low-power TTL needed relatively low resistances, so a common sheet resistance was fine. Precision analog parts moved to laser trimming and, later, to scaled 'valley' resistors.

facts.label: Trimming
facts.value: laser trim for precision; as-deposited for logic

children.name: The nickel-chromium sputtering target
children.description: A block of 80/20 nickel-chromium alloy that the sputter gun erodes. High-purity nickel and chromium are the two metals that dominate this one thin film; the chromium is what gives the film its near-zero temperature coefficient, and the nickel is what makes it resistive rather than metallic.

children.name: The RF/DC sputterer
children.description: A vacuum chamber pumped to a low argon pressure, a cathode holding the NiCr target, the wafer as the anode. An RF or DC glow discharge strikes the target, argon ions knock nickel and chromium atoms loose, and they deposit onto the wafer. It is a slow, line-of-sight, unidirectional process - which is why sputtered NiCr resistors are behind the same shadow problems as sputtered metal interconnect.

children.name: The contact window
children.description: One more mask, which cuts small windows in the field oxide wherever a metal film needs to reach the silicon underneath - the collector, the base, the emitter. Each window is a hole a few micrometres across. The oxide elsewhere is untouched, and it is the oxide that keeps the aluminium from shorting to the substrate everywhere except where you wanted it to.

facts.label: Etch
facts.value: HF through the oxide to the silicon

children.name: Aluminium metallisation
children.description: The final mask. A layer of aluminium about 1 micrometre thick is deposited over the whole wafer - sputtered or evaporated - and a mask removes it everywhere except the wires. Those wires connect the transistor terminals, the resistors, and the bonding pads around the edge of the die. One single metal level, no vias, no second layer. This is the single biggest reason a 1983 logic chip was so simple to make: routing was almost free because the cells were small.
children.note: Single-level aluminium is exactly why bipolar logic with its large cells tolerated one metal layer so well. When bipolar shrank to compete with CMOS it needed two or three metal layers and vias, which is one reason it lost.

children.name: Sintering the metal into the contacts
children.description: After aluminium is deposited, the wafer is pushed briefly to 400-450 C in hydrogen or forming gas. This melts the aluminium into the contact windows, welding it to the silicon and lowering the contact resistance, and it anneals out the sputter damage in the silicon. It is a short, cheap step and it is the reason the metallisation recipe ends with a hydrogen firing.
children.note: Aluminium sintering / hydrogen alloying at 400-450 C was standard in the era. Confidence medium on the exact temperature window; the purpose and the technique are not in doubt.

children.name: Passivation over the metal
children.description: A final film - silicon dioxide, usually with a nitride cap - deposited over the finished aluminium, opened again only at the bonding pads and along the scribe lanes. It seals the chip against moisture and mobile ions, which is what lets a 1983 logic part hold a 15-year life in a consumer television.

children.name: The resulting 3-5 um geometry
children.description: Put together, those four diffusions and the one resistor level put a transistor with a 0.5-1 um base and a 1-2 um emitter sitting inside an isolation island a few tens of micrometres across, wired with 3-5 um aluminium on a single level. That is the '3-5 um minimum feature' of the era's standard bipolar logic line. Compare the dynamic RAM on the same board, patterned at around 1-2 um with two or three aluminium levels and a polysilicon gate - that is where the money was, and that is why the DRAM cost more than the glue.
children.note: The 3-5 um minimum feature is the figure used throughout this tree for 74LS and is standard for early-1980s merchant bipolar logic. The DRAM comparison (~1-2 um, two metal layers) is a reasonable era estimate for a 4164; I have not verified a specific 4164 process cross-section.

children.name: Eight masks, eight photolithography cycles
children.description: A full bipolar logic cycle is repeated for each of its eight mask levels, and each cycle is the same eight or nine operations: clean, dehydrate, spin-coat resist, soft-bake, align and expose, develop, rinse and dry, hard-bake, then inspect - before the wafer goes back to the furnace, the etcher or the implanter. Eight masks times about nine operations is roughly seventy lithography operations, plus oxidation, etching and deposition steps that need no resist, giving the sixty-to-a-hundred total front-end steps.
children.note: The mask set and its order in this tree: (1) isolation, (2) base, (3) NiCr resistor, (4) emitter, (5) contact window, (6) aluminium metal, (7) passivation window, plus the scribe/alignment level - about eight, ordering within the tree illustrative. Every mask is exposed once per wafer batch, and the whole flow through the diffusion and photolithography areas takes a batch of wafers roughly a week to ten days.

children.name: The mask set
children.description: A set of eight photomasks, one per level, each a square of glass about 15 cm on a side with the pattern for that level in opaque chrome. They are made once from the circuit layout, then used to print thousands of wafers. Making the mask set - patterning, mask inspection, and a few days of lead time - was itself a multi-thousand-dollar, multi-week undertaking, and the masks were the physical embodiment of the design.

children.name: The mask blank (soda-lime glass)
children.description: A plate of low-expansion borosilicate or soda-lime glass, polished flat to a few micrometres over 150 mm. Low-expansion glass (LE glass) was preferred for masks because it did not change size with temperature. Both the blank and the pattern ultimately derive from fused silica.

children.name: The opaque chrome layer
children.description: A layer of chromium, evaporated or sputtered onto the glass and then patterned by a mask writer. Chrome is used because it is opaque to the deep-UV and because it survives repeated contact printing without wearing. The clear areas are just bare glass, which is why a mask is easy to inspect: you look through it.

children.name: The reticle (1:1 mask)
children.description: A bipolar logic wafer of 1983 was almost always patterned 1:1 by contact or proximity printing, so the mask carried the pattern at full size - a 100 mm wafer printed from a 100 mm mask. Reticles in the sense of 4x or 5x reduction masks were for steppers and mostly for the finer NMOS and DRAM processes, not for the coarse logic line.
children.note: The distinction: contact/proximity printing needs a full-size mask; a 1:1 projection stepper also prints 1:1 but optically; only a reduction stepper (2x-10x) needs a smaller reticle. Bipolar logic in 1983 was 1:1 by either contact or 1:1 projection. Bipolar logic generally did not use reduction steppers at this node.

children.name: The mask writer
children.description: A computer-controlled plotter that draws the pattern onto the chrome layer - a direct-write electron-beam or laser writer, or a mask stepper using photographic reduction for the simpler logic geometries. The mask set for one part number was the output of days of the mask shop's finest-resolution tool, and it was checked by eye under a microscope before use.
children.note: For 3-5 um logic geometries, a photographic mask stepper was adequate and much faster than electron-beam writing; beam writing was reserved for the DRAM and custom-chip masks.

children.name: Spinning on the resist
children.description: The wafer is put on a vacuum chuck in a bowl, a few millilitres of resist is dispensed, and the bowl spins at several thousand rpm, flinging the resist into a film of a chosen thickness - thicker where a thick layer is needed to etch deep, thinner where fine resolution is needed. The film is then soft-baked to drive off solvent and stabilise the image.

children.name: The coater/developer track
children.description: A machine with hot plates and spray-heads that automates spin-coat, soft-bake, develop, rinse and bake for a whole cassette of wafers in one pass. The track was the workhorse of the photomask bay: an operator loaded a cassette and pushed a button, and the bay's lithography throughput was set by how many tracks it had.

facts.label: Track throughput
facts.value: ~25 wafers per cycle, ~1 min per cycle

children.name: Negative (image-reversing) resist
children.description: On a bipolar line in 1983, resist was still commonly negative: exposure cross-links the resist so it becomes insoluble in the developer, so the pattern left on the wafer after develop is the complement of the mask. This suits diffusion, where you want to open the mask where the oxide is. Positive resists, which behave the intuitive way, had taken over NMOS and CMOS from the late 1970s but lingered on bipolar.
children.note: By 1983 positive resists were already dominant for MOS processes (Shipley AZ-1350 and its successors), and the trend to positive resist across all processes was well advanced; negative resist on bipolar logic persisted into the 1980s. I have stated this as medium confidence on the specific mix in a given vendor's logic bay.

children.name: Dehydration bake before the resist
children.description: Resist will not stick to a wet wafer, so before every coat the wafer goes on a hot plate or in a dehydration oven at 150-250 C to drive off the adsorbed water from the previous wet step. Skipping it causes the single most common resist defect - the film lifting off in patches during development. Every one of the eight cycles repeats this.

children.name: The dehydration hot plate
children.description: A temperature-controlled aluminium or ceramic plate the cassette sits on for a minute or two at 150-200 C. Cheap, essential, and present at every wet bench in the bay.

children.name: Aligning the mask to the wafer
children.description: The wafer is dried, loaded onto a vacuum or magnetic chuck, and the mask is laid directly on top of it - contact printing - or held just above it with a controlled air gap - proximity printing - or imaged one-to-one through a lens. The machine's job is to align each feature on the mask to the feature already printed on the wafer, usually by optically reading alignment marks etched into the previous level. At 3-5 um, alignment tolerance was generous; at DRAM geometries it was brutal.
children.note: Contact printing was cheapest and fastest but printed mask defects onto every die and wore the mask; proximity printing added an air gap for a small resolution penalty. 1:1 projection steppers (like TI's Micralign, and Perkin-Elmer's) were arriving in the early 1980s and gave a clean image without contact wear. Bipolar logic at 3-5 um was comfortable with any of the three.

facts.label: Alignment
facts.value: optical, on marks from previous levels

facts.label: Exposure
facts.value: mercury g-line 436 nm or h-line 405 nm

children.name: The contact/proximity mask aligner
children.description: A granite or cast base, a Chuck/Hamble wafer stage with micrometer knobs for theta and X-Y, a vacuum frame to pull the mask down onto the wafer, a mercury lamp below, and a pair of binocular microscopes to watch the alignment marks. One operator could run one or two of these, spending most of the cycle walking up and down the level stack.

children.name: The 1:1 projection stepper
children.description: A mask aligner that images the mask through a fixed 1:1 lens onto the wafer with a small gap, so there is no contact and no wear, and no mask-defect printing. TI's Micralign and Perkin-Elmer's units of the late 1970s and early 1980s brought this to the logic lines. It was the technology that eventually killed contact printing entirely.

children.name: The mercury lamp
children.description: A 1000 W high-pressure mercury arc with a quartz envelope. Its spectrum peaks at 365, 405 and 436 nm; optical filters select one line, almost always 436 nm (g-line) for the finest resolution the era could reach. Newer deep-UV lamps added 248 nm. The lamp is run at constant power because the resist's exposure depends on its intensity, and lamp ageing was a constant yield headache.

children.name: Developing the image
children.description: The exposed wafer is sprayed with an alkaline developer - for a positive resist, a solution of tetramethylammonium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide; for a negative resist, an organic solvent. The unexposed (positive) or exposed (negative) resist dissolves, leaving the pattern in hardened resist. Then a rinse in deionised water, a dry, and a hard-bake to cross-link the remaining resist so it survives the etch that follows.

children.name: The alkaline developer
children.description: Aqueous alkali, traditionally potassium hydroxide or, from the late 1970s, tetramethylammonium hydroxide. It dissolves the unexposed novolac resin of a positive resist but leaves the exposed, cross-linked, imaged resin alone. TMAH was preferred because it left no metal ion residues that would poison the device.

children.name: Potassium hydroxide (caustic potash)
children.description: The strong alkali in the developer, made by the chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine alongside chlorine. It is the chemical that develops a positive photoresist.

children.name: Brine feed to the chlor-alkali cell
children.description: Concentrated sodium chloride solution, electrolysed to give sodium hydroxide (the alkali), hydrogen and chlorine gas. The same rock salt that makes the epoxy precursors makes the resist developer.

children.name: Rock salt (halite)
children.description: The sodium chloride mined from halite or evaporated from brine. The root of both the chlorine chemistry and the sodium-hydroxide chemistry that strip, develop and etch the resist away.

children.name: Etching the oxide window
children.description: The patterned resist is the stencil; the wafer goes into an etchant. Buffered oxide etch - hydrofluoric acid buffered with ammonium fluoride - attacks the silicon dioxide where the resist is gone, opening the window, and stops at the silicon or at the oxide-nitride beneath. The wafer comes out with resist still on it, which is stripped next. In this era the oxide etch was still wet chemistry; dry plasma etching had not yet replaced it for the bulk oxide.
children.note: Plasma (reactive ion) etching of silicon dioxide was introduced in the early-to-mid 1980s and became standard later in the decade; a 1983 bipolar logic line used wet HF and BOE for its diffusion and contact windows.

facts.label: Selectivity
facts.value: etches SiO2, stops at Si and Si3N4

children.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) - the ore of hydrofluoric acid
children.description: Hydrofluoric acid is made by treating fluorspar, calcium fluoride, with concentrated sulphuric acid in a lead or cast-iron retort at 200-250 C. Fluorspar is dug from hard-rock deposits, notably in Derbyshire and the Ilkley Moor field in England, Mexico, South Africa and China, and it is the single feedstock behind all the oxide etching in the entire semiconductor industry.

facts.label: Main 1980s sources
facts.value: Mexico, South Africa, Spain, China, England

children.name: Limestone (CaCO3)
children.description: The acid side of the HF process, and the source of the calcium sulfate byproduct. Limestone is quarried limestone, chemically calcium carbonate, and it is one of the most widely mined rocks on earth.

children.name: Stripping the resist
children.description: With the etch done, the resist has served its purpose and is removed. The wafer goes into a hot organic solvent - historically xylene or trichloroethylene, later the piranha acid clean. In this era, because resist was often negative and organic, a chlorinated solvent strip in a hot bath was standard. Solvent stripping leaves ionic residue that had to be followed by a piranha clean, a rinse, and a dehydration bake before the next coat.
children.note: Trichloroethylene was ubiquitous as a resist strip in this period and was being phased out for toxicity and ozone reasons through the 1980s, replaced by perchloroethylene and then by piranha (H2SO4/H2O2) wet strips.

children.name: Trichloroethylene solvent strip
children.description: A dense chlorinated solvent, 1,1,1-trichloroethane family, that dissolves the polymerised resist. Boiling in a hot bath it strips the wafer. It is a heavy, volatile, toxic chlorinated hydrocarbon made by chlorinating ethylene and destroying hydrogen chloride with chlorine - another chlorine branch of the tree.
children.note: Trichloroethylene (CHCl=CCl2) specifically, and its 1,1,1-trichloroethane cousins, were the standard resist and degreasing solvents of the era. Being phased out by regulation through the 1980s.

children.name: Ethylene from the cracker
children.description: The other half of the chlorinated-solvent chemistry. Ethylene came from the same steam cracker as the propylene that made the epoxy, from naphtha or from ethane off natural gas. The epoxy body of the package and the solvent that stripped the resist are siblings from one cracker.

children.name: Naphtha feed
children.description: The light hydrocarbon fraction of crude oil distillation, cracked to ethylene and propylene. Every chlorinated organic solvent and every epoxy in this tree comes from this one feed.

children.name: Crude oil
children.description: The root hydrocarbon: the source of the resist solvents, the epoxy, the photoresist binders and the natural gas that made the hydrogen.

children.name: Piranha clean (H2SO4 + H2O2)
children.description: A hot mix of concentrated sulphuric acid and hydrogen peroxide that oxidises organic residue to carbon dioxide and leaves a chemically clean, ion-free surface. Mixed in the fab at the wet bench, it is the standard clean before every photoresist coat and after every resist strip, and it is what made adhesion and ion control reliable.

children.name: Sulphuric acid from sulphur
children.description: Made by burning sulphur or hydrogen sulfide and absorbing in water. Sulphur itself came overwhelmingly from recovered petroleum - the sour crude 'sour gas' processing plants removed hydrogen sulfide from crude and Claus-processed it into elemental sulphur. So the acid that cleans the wafer also traces to crude oil.
children.note: In 1980s practice most industrial sulphur was recovered from oil and gas processing (Claus process) rather than mined, so this path is a strong but not exclusive claim.

children.name: Elemental sulphur (recovered)
children.description: Yellow solid recovered from hydrogen sulfide in oil and gas refining by the Claus process, or mined. Oxidised to sulphur dioxide and absorbed to make sulphuric acid.

children.name: Hydrogen sulfide from sour crude
children.description: The sour-smelling hydrogen sulfide stripped from oil and gas during refining, which is the raw feed for most of the world's manufactured sulphur.

children.name: The full cycle, counted
children.description: One mask level's cycle, run eight times, with the non-lithography steps interleaved. Written out once: dehydrate, coat, soft-bake, align and expose, develop, rinse, hard-bake, wet-etch, strip, clean - ten operations - then the furnace or the sputterer. Eight levels of ten is about eighty lithography-area operations, plus oxidation and diffusion pushes, plus metallisation, plus test. The brief's 'photolithography cycle count' for a 74LS chip is therefore roughly eight masks, ten steps each.

children.name: The photomask bay (Class 10 cleanroom)
children.description: Coating, exposing and developing happened in a 'yellow room' under filtered mercury light and then in a Class 10 (ISO 4) mini-environment with the aligners under hoods. Whole-body suits were only in the Class 100 (ISO 5) areas and the fab sub-fab; the mask bay and the diffusion bay were usually Class 1000 (ISO 6).
children.note: 1980s class numbering: Class 100 = ISO 5 cleanroom, Class 1000 = ISO 6, Class 10 = ISO 4 (the mini-environment used for the most critical steps). This is the older US 'class' convention, different from the ISO class numbers used today.

children.name: Cleanroom air, filtration and the wet bench
children.description: The whole front end runs in filtered air with positive pressure, and the wet benches - the sinks where wafers are etched and cleaned - were the dirtiest place in the fab and the reason it needed a Class 100 (ISO 5) hood over every one. HEPA-filtered air was blown down continuously; nitrogen and dry air purged the tool chambers; and huge volumes of deionised water and process chemicals flowed through the sinks.

facts.label: Classes used
facts.value: Class 10 (ISO 4) mask bay, Class 100 (ISO 5) sub-fab and diffusion bay, Class 1000 (ISO 6) wet bays

facts.label: Wet benches
facts.value: polypropylene sinks under Class 100 laminar hoods

children.name: The HEPA fan filter unit
children.description: A box of pleated glass-fibre or PTFE media in a sheet-metal housing, blowing filtered air down over the tool at 20-40 air changes an hour. It is the single most numerous object in a 1980s fab - one every few square metres of ceiling - and it is why the whole building was pressurised and why the electricity bill was dominated by fan motors.

children.name: The wet bench
children.description: A row of acid-resistant sinks - quartz or polypropylene - where wafers are rinsed and wet-etched. Because wet chemistry releases acid mist and organic solvent vapour, every wet bench sat under a Class 100 laminar-flow hood and exhausted to a scrubbed stack. The wet bench is the reason a 1980s logic line was not as cheap to run as the 'it is just photolithography' story suggests.

children.name: Bulk process gases
children.description: Nitrogen for purging tool chambers and for the sinter anneal, hydrogen for the metal anneal, and oxygen for oxidation and for ashing photoresist, all piped from a bulk gas farm outside the cleanroom. Dry, filtered nitrogen was also the blow-off gas for every wafer before it entered a hot tool.

children.name: The merchant logic fab that ran the process
children.description: A 1983 merchant logic line was a long building with a linear flow: wafers came in at the front and moved one way through cleaning, oxidation and diffusion, photolithography, etch and metallisation, then out to probe, then to assembly and test at the back. Because a logic process was so repeatable, one fab ran dozens of different part numbers on the same flow, changing only the mask set - which is exactly why the 74LS catalogue was so cheap.
children.note: Described generically. Individual vendors ran it differently - TI in Dallas, Fairchild in Mountain View and Palo Alto, National in Santa Clara, Motorola in Phoenix - and I have not traced which specific plant made Commodore's parts.

children.name: Oxidation and diffusion bay
children.description: The hot end of the fab: tube furnaces for oxidation, source drive-in and anneal, plus the epitaxial reactors. This bay determined the cycle time of the whole line, because a diffusion push is hours and a furnace boat takes 20-40 wafers. An operator loaded boats in and out at a slow, deliberate rhythm all shift.

children.name: Photomask bay
children.description: Coaters, developers, aligners and the inspection stations, under Class 10 and Class 100 cleanroom. This was the largest bay by machine count and the largest by electricity draw after the cleanroom air.

children.name: Metallisation bay
children.description: The vacuum tool room: the sputterers that lay down the NiCr resistors and the aluminium metal, the evaporation stations, the sinter furnace, and the ion-implantation machines. Vacuum and cleanroom in one room; argon flows constantly.

children.name: Fab utilities: water, power, scrubbers
children.description: A logic fab in 1983 drew tens of megawatts and consumed tens of millions of gallons of ultrapure water a year, and every acid vapour had to be scrubbed.
