The ultrapure water plant - reverse osmosis then ion exchange, then a final 0.2 um filter - was as large and as capital-intensive as any single machine in the fab.
children.note: The scale figures are order-of-magnitude for a large logic fab, not verified for a specific plant. Water intensity for semiconductors is high relative to most manufacturing; this is well documented generally.

children.name: Where the silicon came from
children.description: No fab makes its own silicon. A logic fab in 1983 bought polished 75 mm or 100 mm wafers from a specialist supplier - Shin-Etsu, Sumitomo, Siltron, MEMC - who themselves bought metallurgical silicon, made it into trichlorosilane or silane, reduced that to polysilicon, pulled a monocrystalline boule by the Czochralski method, and sliced, lapped and polished it. This is the longest supply chain in the whole computer.

children.name: Metallurgical silicon from quartz and coke
children.description: The bottom of the silicon chain. Quartz - silicon dioxide, usually mined as high-purity quartzite - is mixed with coke and heated in a submerged-arc electric furnace at about 2000 C. The carbon reduces the oxide, and molten silicon collects at the bottom: metallurgical silicon, 98-99.5 percent pure. Every silicon wafer in the world begins here.

children.name: Petroleum coke (the carbon reductant)
children.description: The carbon that does the reducing. Petroleum coke is the heavy solid residue left from a refinery coker, essentially the same residuum that feeds the carbon-black furnace. It is mixed into the quartz charge as a reductant and, in the electric furnace, as a source of heat when it burns.

children.name: Crude oil (refinery residue)
children.description: The refinery that makes the coke is fed by crude oil. So the carbon that reduces quartz into silicon came, one step removed, from the same crude oil that made the epoxy, the resist solvents and the natural gas.

children.name: The submerged-arc electric furnace
children.description: A steel shell lined with refractory, with three graphite electrodes plunging into a charge of crushed quartz and coke. An arc between the electrodes melts the mix; the carbon reduces the silicon dioxide and the carbon monoxide gas burns at the electrode tips, superheating the bath to about 2000 C. Molten silicon (99 percent pure) taps off the bottom. A single furnace makes tens of thousands of tonnes of metallurgical silicon a year.

children.name: High-purity quartzite (the ore of silicon dioxide)
children.description: The silica must be unusually pure, because every impurity in the metallurgical silicon becomes a lifetime in the transistor. High-grade quartzite or vein quartz, low in iron and aluminium, is selected - from the Spruce Pine district in North Carolina, from Norway, from the Ural, from Brazil and China. It is crushed and reacted to make trichlorosilane, which is purified by careful redistillation before it ever becomes wafer silicon.
children.note: The shared metal.silica node covers the deeper bauxite-to-oxide chemistry; this node covers the silicon-specific mining and purification requirement of quartz for semiconductor silicon.

children.name: Polysilicon from the Siemens process
children.description: Metallurgical silicon is first reacted with hydrogen chloride at about 300 C to make trichlorosilane (SiHCl3), which is purified by fractional distillation. The purified trichlorosilane is then reduced with pure hydrogen at 1000-1150 C in a fluidised-bed reactor, and fine polycrystalline silicon ('polysilicon') grows on silicon seed particles. The Siemens process - the reaction invented at Siemens in 1954 - is how essentially all the world's polysilicon, and so all its silicon wafers, were made in 1983.

facts.label: Purification
facts.value: fractional distillation of SiHCl3, then reverse cleaning

children.name: Hydrochloric acid (for the trichlorosilane step)
children.description: Hydrochloric acid reacts with the metallurgical silicon to make the trichlorosilane gas. HCl was made from chlorine and hydrogen, or from brine, or bought as a bulk chemical. It is the same chlorine chemistry that makes the epoxy precursors and the resist solvents.

children.name: Chlorine gas
children.description: Chlorine for the hydrochlorination step, from the chlor-alkali cell on brine, with hydrogen from the same cell. The classic industrial pairing.

children.name: Brine
children.description: Concentrated salt solution electrolysed to chlorine, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen.

children.name: Rock salt
children.description: Halite, mined or evaporated from seawater. Root of the chlorine chemistry underneath the silicon, the epoxy and the solvents.

children.name: Hydrogen for the reduction
children.description: High-purity hydrogen reduces the trichlorosilane to silicon in the Siemens reactor. It was made largely by steam reforming of natural gas, with a final purification (molecular sieve and cryogenic adsorption) to get to the parts-per-billion impurity levels the polysilicon needed.

children.name: The hydrogen was mostly natural gas
children.description: By the 1980s the vast majority of the world's hydrogen for ammonia and for electronics was made by steam reforming natural gas - passing methane over a hot nickel catalyst with steam to give hydrogen and carbon monoxide, then shifting and scrubbing. This is the deepest tie in the whole tree: the natural gas that reduced the silicon came out of the same subsurface reservoir complex that the industry calls gas, and methane is the simplest hydrocarbon.

children.name: Methane (natural gas)
children.description: CH4, the dominant component of natural gas, the simplest hydrocarbon. It was reacted with steam over a nickel reforming catalyst at 800-900 C: CH4 + H2O -> CO + 3H2. A shift reactor then converts the carbon monoxide to more hydrogen. This hydrogen reduces the trichlorosilane into pure silicon.

children.name: Natural gas (field)
children.description: Methane and light hydrocarbons drawn from a gas or oil field. This is the geological end of the chemistry: ancient buried organic matter, converted by heat and pressure over geological time into oil and natural gas, and now drawn out of the ground.

children.name: How natural gas formed
children.description: Buried ancient organic sediment, compressed and heated over millions of years by the weight of overburden, cracked into hydrocarbons. Methane is the lightest and most abundant product. This is the true root of the carbon in the computer: the natural gas that made the hydrogen that reduced the silicon that every transistor is built on.

children.name: The gas field
children.description: A reservoir of porous sandstone sealed under an impermeable cap, drilled vertically and produced through a christmas tree of valves, then gathered into a trunk pipeline system. This is where the chain physically ends: a hole in the ground in West Texas, the North Sea, the Dutch Groningen field or the Urengoy field in Siberia, with a gas treatment plant at the wellhead stripping out the hydrogen sulphide and the higher hydrocarbons that would poison a reforming catalyst a few thousand miles downstream.

children.name: Nickel reforming catalyst
children.description: The steam reformer is a bank of tubes packed with nickel on an alumina support. The nickel - from nickel ore - catalyses the methane-steam reaction at 800-900 C. A drop of this catalyst is one more place nickel enters the tree, alongside the NiCr resistor and the lead frame.

children.name: The Siemens fluidised-bed reactor
children.description: A steel vessel with a perforated plate, fluidised with purified hydrogen, into which trichlorosilane vapour is injected alongside seed silicon particles. On the hot (silicon-coated) walls the reaction deposits polycrystalline silicon as fine powder; the powder falls out the bottom. Twenty to thirty tonnes of polysilicon a year came out of one reactor in this era.

children.name: Czochralski growth of the single crystal
children.description: The polysilicon powder is melted with a dopant in a silica crucible at about 1420 C, just above the silicon melting point of 1414 C. A small seed crystal on a puller is dipped in and withdrawn at 1-3 mm/min, rotating. Silicon solidifies on the seed in the melt's lattice, producing a slowly tapering cylinder of near-perfect single crystal called a boule. Arsenic or phosphorus is added to set the wafer's conductivity type and resistivity.

children.name: The Czochralski puller
children.description: A tall crystal-growth machine: a graphite-heated crucible with a rotating seed shaft, a slurry of dopant, an argon atmosphere over the melt, and a diameter-control algorithm watching the melt's edge by laser/weight. It is the machine that turns dirty powder into the perfect single crystal every silicon chip in the world is cut from.

children.name: The fused-silica crucible
children.description: The melt is held in a crucible of fused quartz - amorphous silicon dioxide - because quartz melts above 1600 C and, crucially, because it introduces only oxygen and silicon, both harmless in the crystal, unlike a metal or nitride crucible. The crucible itself is made by flame-fusing pure silica in a hydrogen-oxygen flame, so even the vessel the silicon is melted in comes from the same quartz as the metallurgical silicon.

children.name: The seed crystal
children.description: A small, already-perfect single crystal - usually a few mm across and a few cm long - lowered into the melt to start the growth. Everything that follows inherits its lattice. The seed was itself cut from an earlier boule, so this is a lineage that goes back, crystal generation by crystal generation, to the first Ingot in 1950s.

children.name: Sawing the boule into wafers
children.description: The boule is ground to mark where each wafer will be, then an idling saw - a thin rotating diamond-impregnated steel blade - cuts it, losing up to a millimetre of silicon kerf per cut. A 100 mm boule gave roughly 300 wafers per metre of ingot. Wafers were then lapped flat and parallel, and finally polished mirror-bright.

facts.label: Blade
facts.value: steel or resinoid with diamond grit

facts.label: Kerf
facts.value: 0.2-1.0 mm of silicon lost per wafer

children.name: Industrial diamond
children.description: The abrasive in the saw blade, the scribe and the CMP slurry. Synthesised from graphite under high pressure and temperature in a diamond press, or mined. Graphite itself is carbon, from coal or petroleum coke - another carbon branch off the crude.

children.name: Lapping and edge-rounding
children.description: The wafers are lapped against each other in a slurry to take the bow out of the sawn surface and make them parallel to within microns, then the sharp sawn edge is rounded off with a diamond wheel. The rounded edge is what stops the wafer cracking when it is chucked onto the probe stage and spun through the photolithography coater.

children.name: Lapping slurry
children.description: A slurry of loose diamond or alumina grit in water, to grind the wafer flat. The abrasive is the same industrial mineral as the blade.

children.name: Final polish
children.description: A final, slow, chemically-assisted polish takes the lapped surface to a mirror finish, because every speck of damage left on the surface becomes a defect that kills transistors. A sacrificial thermal oxide is then grown on the polished surface and stripped, which anneals the last of the surface damage - the 'getter' that heals the crystal's outermost lattice layer.

children.name: 3-inch and 4-inch wafers in 1983
children.description: Standard wafer diameters in 1983 were 3 inches (75 mm) and 4 inches (100 mm); 5-inch (125 mm) was arriving at the leading-edge logic and memory lines. A 4-inch wafer holds roughly 1,500-3,000 of the small dies that a 14-pin logic part becomes, depending on die size and the edge exclusion the process could hold.
children.note: Die-per-wafer for a 14-pin logic die (a few square mm) on a 100 mm wafer does land in the 1,000-3,000 range by straightforward area arithmetic, but I have not verified a specific published figure for 74LS in 1983. The wafer diameters are high confidence.

children.name: Die-per-wafer economics
children.description: The economics of a merchant logic wafer rest entirely on this number: how many working dies of one part number come off a wafer. Multiply by yield, multiply by the cost of the wafer, divide by the dies, and you have the die cost - which for a 74LS gate is dominated not by the wafer but by testing, packaging and the fixed cost of the masks and the fab, amortised over millions of gates.
children.note: The 1,500-3,000 figure is an area calculation and is plausible for a 14-pin die on a 4-inch wafer; it is not a sourced measurement. Confidence medium.

facts.label: Yield at probe
facts.value: varies widely; the margin between good and scrap dies is what testing must find

children.name: What happened to bipolar logic afterwards
children.description: The 74LS line described here is essentially extinct as a manufacturing process. CMOS won because it drew almost no static power, scaled, and could hold a whole microprocessor on one die, which bipolar could never do economically. Bipolar survives only in niches: high-voltage, high-current, precision-analog and microwave parts, where the bipolar transistor's current handling and gain are still hard to beat. The two families also merged into BiCMOS.

children.name: Where bipolar still survives
children.description: Power regulators, high-voltage controllers, low-dropout rectifiers, precision amplifiers, the front end of high-speed analog, microwave amplifiers, Hall sensors. Bipolar transistors are still grown epitaxially and still use guard rings and deep-trench isolation at the very leading edge - the process family survived, the market for plain logic gates in it did not.

children.name: BiCMOS - bipolar and CMOS on one wafer
children.description: A process that builds CMOS logic and bipolar output drivers on the same die: the CMOS for low power and density, the bipolar for high current drive on the outputs. It was used in some gate arrays and in the output stages of older CPUs, and it was abandoned once CMOS itself could drive high current enough. It is the process family that merged the two halves of this branch.
children.note: BiCMOS was real and used through the 1980s-1990s (for example in some gate arrays and cache parts) and is now largely gone from production. Confidence medium on where exactly it was used; high that the process family existed and later declined.

children.name: The 3-5 um feature, then and now
children.description: The 3-5 um minimum feature of this logic line is unrecognisably coarse today. Modern advanced logic runs at nanometre nodes with hundreds of millions of transistors per die, whereas a 74LS gate has of the order of a few dozen transistors in total. The geometry went from the thousands of transistors that fit on one 100 mm wafer of glue logic to the billions that now fit on one 300 mm wafer of a GPU. Nothing about the aluminium DIP package, the epoxy, the lead frame or the DIP pin spacing changed at all through that entire scaling - only the silicon inside.

facts.label: Unchanged
facts.value: DIP package, epoxy, lead frame, 0.1 in pitch

children.name: The CMOS half: 4066, MC4044, 74LS629
children.description: Three of the C64's glue chips are CMOS, and they were made on a completely different line from the 74LS parts. Instead of four diffusion cycles and an epitaxial collector, a CMOS line does a p-well and an n-well implant, grows a field oxide between them by LOCOS, grows a hundred-nanometre gate oxide, deposits polysilicon, and uses that same polysilicon as its own mask for the source and drain implant. Roughly ten mask levels, no epitaxy, no gold, no NiCr resistor film, and a static power consumption of nanowatts instead of milliwatts. That combination is why CMOS took the whole logic business within fifteen years.
children.note: Describes a 3-5 um n-well/p-well twin-tub CMOS process with LOCOS isolation, self-aligned source/drain and a single aluminium level - the mainstream logic CMOS of 1982-84, and the process behind the RCA/Motorola 4000-series and the early 74HC. TI's Micralign lines, Fairchild's and National's equivalent lines, and the Japanese and Korean fabs all ran something close to this. Two details are period-specific: LOCOS was still the isolation of choice (shallow-trench isolation was arriving but not yet dominant), and the 4000-series parts such as the 4066 and MC4044 were older designs that typically used a simpler, single-well or p-well-only CMOS rather than a full twin-tub. Confidence medium because the exact flow of a given vendor's 4000-series part is proprietary.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: n-well / p-well twin-tub CMOS, LOCOS isolation

facts.label: Minimum feature
facts.value: 3-5 um (same node as the bipolar logic line)

facts.label: Gate
facts.value: polysilicon over ~100 nm thermal oxide, self-aligned S/D

facts.label: Static power
facts.value: nW per gate vs ~2 mW for a 74LS gate

children.name: The twin-tub CMOS flow
children.description: The order of a CMOS process is dictated by one rule: you can never put anything back into silicon after a high-temperature step, so everything that must survive later furnace work is done first, in descending order of temperature. Wells, then field oxide, then thin gate oxide, then polysilicon, then the self-aligned source/drain implants at a low temperature, then metal.

children.name: p-type substrate (and the tub)
children.description: The wafer is p-type, lightly doped. On top of it two wells are implanted: a deep n-well and a somewhat shallower p-well. The n-well holds every p-channel transistor; the p-well (or the substrate itself, on simpler parts) holds every n-channel transistor. Two tubs, two polarities, one chip - that is the 'twin tub'. The wells must be deep enough that they do not punch through into each other and short the two transistor types together.

children.name: n-well and p-well implants
children.description: Two masked implants. Phosphorus (or arsenic) goes into the n-well; boron into the p-well. At 3-5 um these were thermal diffusions or, increasingly, implantations - by the early 1980s medium-current implanters were displacing diffusion in CMOS, the opposite trend to bipolar, where diffusion survived much longer. An implantation is done cold and fast: the dopant is accelerated into the surface at tens of keV and stops almost where it is put.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: ion implantation (thermal diffusion still in use)

children.name: The medium-current ion implanter
children.description: A big steel vacuum chamber with a source, an analysing magnet, an accelerating column and a beamline down to a scan platter that holds the wafer. The dopant is ionised, selected by mass, accelerated to tens of keV, and swept across the wafer. Implanters were expensive, and CMOS was the process that made them a standard line tool rather than a special one.
children.note: Implanters were standard in CMOS lines by the early 1980s; diffusion was still the workhorse in bipolar logic, which is one of the more interesting differences between the two processes.

children.name: LOCOS isolation
children.description: Locally Oxidised Silicon. Where two transistors must not touch, the field oxide is simply grown. A layer of silicon nitride is deposited and patterned; the wafer is oxidised in steam, so oxide grows everywhere the nitride is absent; the nitride is stripped off in hot phosphoric acid, leaving a thick field oxide behind. It is isolation by oxidising rather than by doping, and it is the reason a CMOS chip looks like a quilt of raised oxide platforms.

facts.label: Mask oxide
facts.value: Si3N4, LPCVD from silane and ammonia

facts.label: Known problem
facts.value: the 'bird's beak' - the field oxide grows sideways and eats into the active area

children.name: The silicon nitride masking film
children.description: A layer of amorphous silicon nitride, deposited by low-pressure chemical vapour deposition from silane and ammonia at about 800 C. It is used in three places in a CMOS line: as the mask that protects active areas during field oxidation, as the encapsulant under the nitride passivation at the end, and as a spacer. Nitride is chosen because it is immune to hot steam - which is precisely why it is a good mask for something that is about to be steamed.

children.name: Ammonia (NH3)
children.description: The nitrogen source for the nitride. In 1983 essentially all industrial ammonia was made by the Haber-Bosch process: nitrogen from the air plus hydrogen from steam-reformed natural gas, over an iron catalyst at 400-500 C and 200-300 atm. So the mask that defines a CMOS transistor's isolation runs, indirectly, on natural gas.

children.name: Nitrogen from the air
children.description: The other half of Haber-Bosch: air separated by cryogenic distillation or pressure-swing adsorption into nitrogen and oxygen. 78 percent of the atmosphere, liquefied at one atmosphere only at 77 K, which is why air separation plants are enormous cryogenic plants.

children.name: Air
children.description: 78 percent nitrogen, 21 percent oxygen, 1 percent argon and carbon dioxide. The raw material for every cubic metre of ammonia, and therefore of every silicon nitride masking film, in the world.

children.name: Hydrogen for the ammonia
children.description: Steam-reformed methane, exactly the hydrogen that reduces the trichlorosilane into polysilicon. Two branches of the same industrial gas meet here: one gas becomes silicon, the other becomes the mask that patterns it.

children.name: Hot phosphoric acid for the nitride strip
children.description: Silicon nitride is attacked by hot concentrated phosphoric acid and by nothing else practical, so a boiling phosphoric acid bath is the standard way to remove it. The acid was made by burning phosphorus - itself from phosphate rock - in excess air and absorbing the oxide in water.
children.note: The chemistry is high confidence; the specific tank temperature (~150-180 C) is a standard process figure but I have not verified a 1983 datasheet for it.

children.name: The gate oxide
children.description: Inside the active windows the thin gate oxide is grown, by dry oxidation in oxygen at about 1000 C. On a 3-5 um part it is 80-120 nm thick - a few hundred atom layers. This film is the transistor: its thickness sets the threshold voltage and its capacitance sets the drive current, and it is the thinnest and most fragile thing on the chip. At 1983's feature sizes it was still thick by modern standards, which is one reason CMOS of that era was not yet faster than bipolar.

children.name: The polysilicon gate
children.description: A layer of polycrystalline silicon is deposited over the whole wafer, then doped (usually with phosphorus from phosphine, or with POCL3 in a furnace) so that it conducts, then patterned. That patterned polysilicon is the gate. Crucially, it is also used as the mask for the source and drain implant immediately afterwards - so the gate aligns itself, and no extra mask is needed. The self-aligned gate and source/drain, invented at Fairchild in the late 1960s, is the single idea that made CMOS manufacturable at all.

facts.label: Doping
facts.value: phosphine in the deposition, or POCL3 furnace

children.name: Silane (SiH4) as the polysilicon feed
children.description: Silane decomposes on a hot surface at 700-850 C to lay down pure polycrystalline silicon. It is a cleaner and more controllable feed than trichlorosilane - no chlorine, no corrosive by-products - and by the early 1980s it was becoming the preferred source for polysilicon deposition in CMOS even though trichlorosilane still dominated for boule-grade silicon.
children.note: Silane was used for polysilicon deposition from roughly the mid-1970s onward. Confidence medium on the exact balance between silane and dichlorosilane in 1983 CVD; the trichlorosilane-versus-silane split for boule-grade silicon (trichlorosilane dominant) is high confidence.

facts.label: Also called
facts.value: monosilane; the gaseous form of 'silicon hydride'

children.name: The self-aligned source and drain
children.description: With the gate already patterned in polysilicon, the source and drain are implanted straight through the exposed silicon beside it, and the gate itself blocks the implant everywhere it is. No alignment mask is needed: the gate defines the gap between source and drain by its own edge. Two implants, phosphorus for the n-channel source/drain and boron for the p-channel, each masked by the opposite field oxide. This is 'self-aligned', and it is the reason a CMOS transistor's channel length is set by a printed line width and nothing else.

facts.label: Masking
facts.value: the polysilicon gate itself, plus the opposite field oxide

children.name: The source/drain anneal
children.description: After the implant the wafer goes back into a furnace briefly to heal the crystal damage and to activate the dopant atoms into substitutional positions. This is the one remaining high-temperature step, and it is why CMOS still used a furnace in the era when bipolar was moving to implantation.
children.note: The activation anneal was around 800-900 C for an hour, or a rapid thermal anneal of a few seconds at 1000 C plus. Medium confidence on the exact numbers.

children.name: Contact and aluminium interconnect
children.description: The field oxide is etched away over the source, drain and gate to expose silicon, then aluminium is deposited and patterned into one single layer of interconnect. Exactly the same metallisation as the bipolar line, exactly the same problems (step coverage over the oxide steps, electromigration under current) and exactly the same solution in this era: one level, because at 3-5 um the cells were big enough to route around with a single layer.

children.name: Passivation, and why CMOS needed less of it
children.description: An interlayer oxide and a final nitride cap, opened only at the pads and scribe lanes. A CMOS device is far less sensitive to mobile ions than a bipolar one, because a CMOS gate draws no gate current and its threshold is set electrostatically rather than by charge state; so the passivation job is easier and the nitride does most of the work.
children.note: The relative immunity of CMOS to mobile charge is standard device physics; the specific passivation stack comparison is a reasonable generalisation rather than a cited measurement.

children.name: Where a 4066 puts its resistors
children.description: The 4000-series CMOS parts rarely needed resistors at all - CMOS logic is naturally high impedance, so biasing resistors are sparse - but the 4066's on-resistance trimmer and some bias chains did use deposited polysilicon resistors at a value set by sheet resistance and length. Poly resistors are cheap to add because they are made at the same time as the gate, from the same film, at no extra mask.
children.note: Low confidence. That a 4066 uses on-chip polysilicon resistors is plausible from its trim and bias requirements but I did not verify a cross-section, and some 4000-series parts use no resistors at all.

children.name: The photolithography is the same, but the resist is positive
children.description: A CMOS line of 1983 reused the same mask aligners, coaters and developers as the bipolar line next door. The one substantive difference is the resist: by the end of the 1970s the NMOS and CMOS lines had already switched to positive resists such as Shipley's AZ-1350, while bipolar logic was still often running negative resists. Positive resists tolerate the small misalignment that LOCOS bird's-beak and oxide steps cause better, which is part of why MOS won.

children.name: Positive photoresist and the end of negative resist
children.description: A positive resist is a novolac resin with a photosensitive protecting group. Exposure breaks the group off, the exposed resin becomes soluble in the alkaline developer, and the pattern on the wafer is the same polarity as the pattern on the mask - no mental inversion, no image reversal, and better control of linewidth on steps. Positive resists went from invention in the 1940s to default in the late 1970s; by 1983 they had won MOS and were displacing negative resist on bipolar. Within a decade negative resist was gone from production lines entirely.

facts.label: Adoption
facts.value: NMOS from late 1970s; all production by early 1990s

children.name: What a CMOS transmission gate is made of
children.description: The 4066's four 'bilateral switches' are the canonical CMOS cell: two MOSFETs of opposite polarity in parallel between two nodes, each with its gate driven by one of the two control inputs. When the control is high the pair conducts in both directions; when it is low the pair is off and the terminals float. It is two transistors. That is the whole reason CMOS logic is cheap - there is no junction isolation, no epitaxy, no resistor film and no gold-doped emitter to reproduce for every function, just NMOS and PMOS.

facts.label: Cell
facts.value: complementary NMOS + PMOS in parallel = transmission gate

facts.label: Bidirectional
facts.value: yes - unlike an NMOS pass transistor

facts.label: On resistance
facts.value: hundreds of ohms to a few kohm

children.name: Where the CMOS parts were made
children.description: The 4066 and MC4044 were Motorola and RCA parts, made in Motorola's own bipolar-compatible CMOS lines and in the Japanese and Southeast Asian fabs that had been built to supply them. By 1983 the merchant CMOS capacity was expanding fast and much of it was in Japan and Korea, where the cost of a CMOS line was falling faster than in the United States.
children.note: Low confidence on the specific plants. I have not traced which fab produced the MC4044 and 4066 in Commodore's 1983 shipments.

children.name: What CMOS became
children.description: The same n-well/p-well/twin-tub idea, shrunk by a factor of thousands. Every design rule changed - shallow trench isolation replaced LOCOS and finally gave way to fin-shaped gates; the gate material changed from polysilicon to metal; the number of copper interconnect layers went from one to a dozen; the light source went from a mercury lamp to an argon fluoride excimer laser at 193 nm, and then to extreme ultraviolet light at 13.5 nm, which needs a vacuum. A 3-5 um logic gate became a nanometre-scale device with billions of its relatives.

facts.label: Exposure
facts.value: 436 nm mercury lamp -> 193 nm ArF -> 13.5 nm EUV

facts.label: Transistors per die
facts.value: ~10 for a 4066 switch; ~10^10 for a modern GPU

children.name: Shallow trench isolation replaced LOCOS
children.description: The bird's beak - the way LOCOS field oxide grew sideways and swallowed the active area - became a scaling killer as geometries shrank. Shallow trench isolation, in which a narrow trench is etched into the substrate and filled with oxide and a nitride liner, gives a much sharper boundary and became universal from the late 1980s onward. It is a direct descendant of the deep-trench-isolation idea described in the bipolar branch.

children.name: Where Commodore's logic chips came from
children.description: Commodore did not fab logic. It bought merchant 74-series parts from the American and Japanese vendors, and because a machine built in millions cannot wait for a part number to be on allocation, it also ran second sources of its own - internal house-numbered equivalents made at other plants, marked 7701, 7707, 7708, 7711, 8712 and so on. An original C64 board may carry parts branded TI, Fairchild, National, Motorola, Hitachi, Toshiba or a Commodore number, all mixed on the same board, all doing the same job.
children.note: The vendor list and the second-source practice are well attested by the physical parts on surviving boards and by Commodore's parts lists. I could not find a primary source naming which plants made Commodore's specific lots, so no plant is claimed below as fact.

facts.label: Named suppliers on a 250407
facts.value: TI, Fairchild, National, Motorola, Hitachi, Toshiba, MOS house numbers

facts.label: Purchase route
facts.value: vendor sales, franchised distributor, and broker / open market

children.name: The merchant logic vendors
children.description: Five or six companies made the overwhelming majority of the world's 74-series logic in the early 1980s. Between them they ran the same public process to the same design rules, which is why a 74LS08 from any of them was interchangeable. What they did not share was quality: this is the core of the C64's running joke that some boards need three attempts before they work.

facts.label: Origins
facts.value: TI invented the 7400; Fairchild, National and Motorola/Signetics cloned and improved it

facts.label: Interchangeability
facts.value: same pinout and function, different vendor mark

children.name: Texas Instruments
children.description: The company that invented the 7400 series in 1964 and the Schottky TTL in 1964-65, and the largest supplier of the 74LS catalogue. It ran its own fabs (among them Dallas, Sugar Land in Texas, and Niceville in Florida) and also did foundry work for others - the fab-forum business was a real cash generator in the era.
children.note: TI's role and the 7400/74S chronology are high confidence. Specific plant names are given as commonly-cited TI locations rather than verified suppliers of Commodore's lots.

facts.label: Extra business
facts.value: foundry / fab-forum for other semiconductor firms

children.name: Fairchild
children.description: The company where Faggin invented the silicon-gate technology that made CMOS practical, in 1968, and which shipped the first commercial silicon-gate MOS ICs. Fairchild went bankrupt in 1985 and its remaining operations were absorbed by National and by a French group, so by 1983 a Fairchild-branded 74LS was already a slightly awkward purchase.
children.note: Fairchild's silicon-gate invention in 1968 and the 1985 bankruptcy are well documented. That Fairchild-branded logic was actually present on C64 boards is field-attested but I did not verify a specific board photograph showing it.

children.name: National Semiconductor
children.description: A major second-source supplier of 74LS logic throughout the period, and the company that published the 74HC/74HCT databooks that turned high-speed CMOS into a genuine 74-series replacement. It later absorbed much of Fairchild.
children.note: National as a 74LS supplier is high confidence. Its 74HC databooks (1983) are a well-documented and interesting artefact - the high-speed CMOS family arriving at the same moment as the C64.

children.name: Motorola and Signetics
children.description: Motorola was the dominant supplier of the 4000-series CMOS parts - the MC4044 and MC4066 on the C64 - and Signetics had been an important TTL second source. The two had been linked by a licensing and cross-supply arrangement since 1969, so both names turned up in the same catalogue.
children.note: Motorola as the MC-prefix supplier of the 4066/4044 is high confidence - that is what the MC prefix means. The Signetics link-up is a well-documented aspect of that era but I have not cited a primary source for it here.

children.name: Hitachi, Toshiba and the Japanese suppliers
children.description: By the mid-1980s Japanese and then Korean vendors had taken a large share of world logic volume, and they were undercutting American silicon hard. C64 boards are also found with Hitachi-branded parts. Commodore bought early and often, and the rising Japanese share was one reason the C64's own bill of materials got cheaper every year of its life.
children.note: Low confidence on specific Japanese parts appearing on 1983 C64 boards. The general Japanese penetration of merchant logic through the decade is well documented; a specific Hitachi-branded 74LS in a 250407 is a field report I did not verify.

children.name: Commodore's own second sources: the 77xx house numbers
children.description: To avoid single-supplier risk Commodore had equivalents of several glue parts made for it and marked with its own house numbers: 7701 and 8701 in place of the PLA family, 7707 for the 7406 hex inverter, 7708 or 7711 for the 74LS139 decoder, and 7712 for the 74LS08 quad AND. These were contracted from other fabs under Commodore's specification. They are functionally equivalent and reliably much worse - the MOS-made decoder and inverter parts are among the most failure-prone components on a C64.
children.note: The house numbers and their equivalents are field-attested in multiple independent repair accounts; the mechanism (contract fabrication of a second source) is the standard reading but I could not find a Commodore primary document describing the practice.

facts.value: equivalent to the 7406 hex inverter at U8
equivalent to the 74LS139 decoder at U15
equivalent to the 74LS08 quad AND at U27

facts.label: Reliability
facts.value: the MOS house-number parts are notably failure-prone

children.name: How the chips physically arrived in 1983
children.description: Nobody at Commodore's Pennsylvania assembly plant picked up a telephone and ordered from Texas Instruments. There was a distribution chain, and where a part sat in that chain decided both its price and whether it was genuine. Buying from the manufacturer's own sales arm or a franchised distributor got you an authorised part with a full warranty and a date code. Buying from a broker or an independent distributor got you the same silicon much cheaper, with no guarantee of origin at all.
children.note: The franchised-versus-independent split, and the grey market that grew out of allocation shortages in the early 1980s, are well documented - the semiconductor industry began formal counterfeiting and diversion programmes in response to exactly this period. What I cannot establish is which route Commodore used for which part, which is exactly the sort of thing that gets litigated decades later.

facts.label: Unauthorised channels
facts.value: independent distributors, brokers, the open market

facts.label: Why it existed
facts.value: allocation shortages, price gaps, and nobody policing small parts

children.name: Allocation and the queue
children.description: When demand exceeded supply - and in 1982-84 it very often did, because the whole consumer electronics industry was recovering from the 1980-81 recession simultaneously - a manufacturer rationed. A computer maker with a purchase order got whatever share the vendor allocated, pro rata, and had to schedule its production around delivery dates rather than around its own. This is why the price of a commodity 74LS was set by the market's shortage rather than by what it cost to make.
children.note: Allocation was standard practice in the 1980-83 shortage period and is well attested; the semiconductor industry's own diversion-fighting literature of the era confirms the shortages were real. Medium confidence on how specifically it applied to Commodore's glue-logic buys.

children.name: Authorised versus unauthorised: the 'pulls'
children.description: Parts that reached a buyer through anything other than a franchised distributor were, in the trade's language, 'pulled'. This could be entirely innocent - a company over-ordered and released surplus, a broker bought at auction - or it could be diverted from a competitor's own allocation. Because a 74LS08 has no serial number, no authentication and no visible origin, nobody could tell the difference. The industry response in the 1980s and 1990s was a growing formal apparatus for tracking authorised distribution, and the counterfeiting industry grew alongside it.
children.note: Medium confidence. The general unauthorised-distribution and counterfeiting environment of the early 1980s is well documented from the industry-response side. Claiming that Commodore's specific parts came through unauthorised channels would need documentary evidence I do not have; the tree deliberately does not claim it.

children.name: Incoming inspection at the Commodore plant
children.description: Every shipment of semiconductors was counted, and the number was checked against the bill of materials before the parts went anywhere near a board. Chips that did not match were quarantined. This is worth noting because the components on a C64 mainboard are not hand-selected: the board either works with whatever chip arrived in the box or it is reworked, which is a large part of why surviving C64s need a recap and a chip-sorting pass before they will run.
children.note: Low confidence. Incoming count and inspection in electronics assembly of this era is a generic, well-attested practice; I have not found a Commodore document describing its incoming test procedure for logic parts.

children.name: What a 74LS is made of, and what it cost
children.description: The whole point of the comparison: a 74LS chip is a few milligrams of silicon, a few milligrams of metal, a third of a gram of epoxy, and a couple of hundred person-minutes of work spread across a fortnight of factory flow time. It sold for a few tens of cents. The 6510 on the same board, a thousand times more transistors with a finer process, cost several dollars. Commodore's entire bill of materials for the electronics was a small fraction of the machine's retail price.
children.note: Confidence low on the numbers and high on the shape of the answer. I could not find a primary 1983 distributor price list for 74LS parts or a documented Commodore purchase price for a 6510, so the price figures below are order-of-magnitude estimates from the general trend of semiconductor price decline and the retail pricing of the era, not measured figures. The material mass estimates are arithmetic from die dimensions and layer thicknesses and should be right to within a factor of a few; the commonly quoted '0.3 g of aluminium' figure for a 14-pin logic chip looks too high for on-die metal by about an order of magnitude and I have said so.

facts.label: Price trend
facts.value: semiconductor prices fell faster than 10%/yr through the 1980s

children.name: Bill of materials for one 74LS04
children.description: An honest accounting of what is actually inside one of these chips, with the arithmetic shown so it can be checked.
children.note: Mass figures are estimates from die area and process layer thicknesses; the on-die aluminium figure is roughly 10-30 mg by arithmetic, which is well below the 0.3 g figure often quoted for these chips. The 0.3 g number is closer to the aluminium that passes through the sputter targets across a whole wafer and is later reclaimed, than to the metal in one finished device.

children.name: Silicon: about 3 mg, not 3-5 um
children.description: The figure usually quoted for a 74-series chip - '3-5 um of silicon' - is the depth of the active junctions, the epitaxial collector plus base plus emitter, which is what a device-physics description means by it. The wafer itself is a 300 um thick slice, and a 74LS04 die of roughly 1.5 by 2.4 mm weighs about 3 mg. So the chip that contains the logic is a few milligrams of crystal and a few hundred of package.
children.note: Die dimensions for a 74LS04 are consistent across the sources I checked (about 1.5 x 2.4 mm); the derived mass is simple arithmetic. Confidence medium because I did not find a measured weight.

children.name: Aluminium: order 10-30 mg on the die
children.description: One single metallisation level about 1.0-1.5 um thick, covering maybe half the die. For a 3.6 mm2 die that is a few cubic millimetres of metal - on the order of 10 to 30 milligrams, not the 0.3 g sometimes quoted. The discrepancy matters because it is the difference between the aluminium in the chip and the aluminium that went through the fab's sputtering equipment to make every chip on every wafer.
children.note: Explicitly flagging a correction to the brief's figure. My arithmetic gives roughly 10-30 mg of aluminium in the finished die; the 0.3 g figure is plausible only if you count the whole evaporated/sputtered inventory later reclaimed. Confidence low because both are estimates, but the order-of-magnitude gap is real.

facts.label: Brief's figure
facts.value: ~0.3 g - probably wafer-level, not per chip

children.name: Gold: under a milligram
children.description: Gold enters twice. About eighteen wire bonds of 0.5-1.0 mil gold wire on a DIP-14 work out at a few tenths of a milligram in total. The die attach preform of gold-silicon eutectic adds a fraction of a milligram more. Together, roughly half a milligram to a milligram of gold per finished chip - and the industry had been actively trying to get rid of it, because gold was one of the two most expensive materials in the package.
children.note: The arithmetic from wire diameter, bond count and bond length is straightforward but unverified against measured data, and the brief's 'few milligrams of gold' is at the top of my own range rather than contradicted by it. Confidence low.

children.name: Nickel-chromium: a film, not a lump
children.description: The thin-film resistors are the only place nickel and chromium appear in the die itself. A thousand or so angstroms of film over a few percent of the die area works out to well under a milligram, so the NiCr is chemically trivial even though it is functionally essential - every pull-up and bias resistor in a 74LS chip is made of it.

children.name: Nickel: mostly in the lead frame, not the chip
children.description: The largest mass of nickel in the whole device is in the lead frame, a strip of 42 percent nickel iron about 0.2 mm thick weighing on the order of 100 mg for a DIP-14, plus the plating. The nickel that matters for supply-chain purposes is in that frame, not in the silicon.

children.name: Epoxy moulding compound: the heaviest part
children.description: By mass the epoxy moulding compound is the largest single material in the chip - 0.3 to 0.6 g of silica-filled thermoset, of which about three quarters is fused silica. The die is a hundredth of the package's weight. That is the whole story of the 1983 IC in one comparison: 3 mg of clever silicon buried in 400 mg of dull polymer, so that the 3 mg could be handled, protected, and plugged into a socket.
children.note: The compound mass range is a standard figure for a small DIP and is reasonably firm; the silica fraction within it is high confidence for era EMC formulations.

children.name: Total weight of a 74LS04
children.description: Roughly half a gram. A thousand chips would weigh half a kilogram; a C64's eleven glue chips weigh about five grams between them. The tree is deep and the material branches multiply, but the object itself is tiny, light and almost entirely plastic.

children.name: How much human time, spread how thin
children.description: The brief's figure of roughly 200 person-minutes per finished chip is the right order of magnitude and worth unpacking, because it is not 200 minutes of one person's attention. It is direct operator and technician time amortised across the whole flow: the ~60-100 front-end steps, most of which run unattended inside a tool cycle of minutes but each of which needs a cassette loaded, a recipe checked, a defect inspection and a wafer-count reconciliation. Front-end and back-end together put the figure in the low hundreds of person-minutes. The rest of the cost was in the fab: capital, cleanroom air, process engineering, and yield learning spread over years and shared across millions of gates.
children.note: This is an order-of-magnitude estimate and I want to be explicit about that. It is broadly consistent with the economics of the era - a commodity logic chip had a manufacturing cost in the tens of cents against a price in the tens of cents - but I have no measured figure from a 1983 fab and I have not attempted to derive one from a cost model. Treat 'about 200 person-minutes' as a defensible intuition rather than a number with a source.

facts.label: Of which back end
facts.value: probe test, assembly, final test, inspection

facts.label: Flow time
facts.value: ~1-2 weeks of factory time, of which minutes are hands-on

children.name: Flow time versus touch time
children.description: The distinction that makes the whole estimate work. A batch of wafers spends a week and a half moving through the fab, and almost all of that time is waiting - in a furnace, in a queue, in a cassette under a nitrogen purge. What costs money is not the waiting; it is the roughly twenty or thirty separate occasions when somebody has to be present and paying attention. Over a fortnight, that is a couple of hours, not a couple of weeks.
children.note: The flow-time-versus-touch-time distinction is the standard batch-fab cost structure and is well established. The specific 1-2 week figure for a full bipolar logic cycle is my estimate and is medium confidence.

children.name: The price gap between the glue and the CPU
children.description: The commercially important fact about the 74-series on the C64 is that it was nearly free. A commodity 74LS gate was priced against a cost of a few tens of cents and a price in the same range, falling year on year as the industry learned. The 6510 was a custom NMOS design on a finer process, and as a custom part on a custom mask set it cost several dollars and could not be shared with anyone. Which is why Commodore's engineers minimised custom silicon and spent money freely on merchant glue - and also why the later C128 could add a second 6510 and a bank-switching PLA without touching the price of the machine.
children.note: Low confidence on the specific figures, high confidence on the ratio and the logic. I could not find a documented 1983 price list for 74LS logic or a Commodore purchase price for a 6510; the numbers quoted are order-of-magnitude estimates. The broader semiconductor price trend - prices falling at roughly 10-30 percent a year in real terms through the early 1980s, faster for commodity logic - is documented in the economic literature and is the basis for the direction even if not the specific prices.

children.name: Why merchant logic was cheaper per function
children.description: A merchant part's cost is amortised across every customer in the world and over a mask set that runs on a flow which makes dozens of other part numbers. Commodore was buying a fraction of the output of a factory that existed whether or not Commodore existed, with a mask set Commodore did not pay for and a design Commodore did not own. The 6510 was the opposite on every count: one mask set, one customer, one buyer, and a design that had to be paid for before it shipped a single unit.
children.note: The amortisation argument for merchant-versus-custom silicon is a standard, well-established argument from the economics of the era rather than a measured figure for these parts.
